"question-3c788761-8a3d-5a84-9fc6-a55521c1f3bb" :question/id #uuid "3c788761-8a3d-5a84-9fc6-a55521c1f3bb" :question/math-academy-id "q-109579" :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 & 2 \\ 5 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $v$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

I. $v$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A$

II. $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A$

III. $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A$" :question/worked-solution "A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{n}$ of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{n}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{n-1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }…\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

First, we compute $A-3I:$

$$
A-3I=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 & 2 \\ 5 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 2 \\ 5 & -4 & 2 \\ 3 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- Next, we find the image of $v$ under the action of $A-3I:$

$$
(A-3I)v=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 2 \\ 5 & -4 & 2 \\ 3 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\ne 0
$$

- Since we got a nonzero vector in the last step, we now compute the image of $w$ under the action of $A-3I:$

$$
(A-3I)w=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 2 \\ 5 & -4 & 2 \\ 3 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=0
$$

So, we obtain the following chain of maps:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{v}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{0}
$$

Here, we see that $A-3I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $2$ steps.

Therefore:

$\,$ *$v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A.$*

So, the correct answer is "III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a676cad1-550b-58ad-bc2d-4c3f63df1e8e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 9 \\ 9 & 0\end{aligned}].$*" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

$$

$$

Therefore, the solution is

Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-3)}\,x(3) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6(t-3)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(6(t-3)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6(t-3)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6(t-3))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6(t-3))\, \\ \,\operatorname{sin}⁡(6(t-3))\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)\,c$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(0)=c$

{{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

$$

$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{properties of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider line $\text{L4}.$ The standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is defined as the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ From line $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

and from line $\text{L4}$ we know ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.$ Replacing ${Φ}_{0}(0)$ with ${I}_{n}$ in the equation $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c$ gives

$$
x(0)={I}_{n}c=c,
$$

which is exactly line $\text{L5}.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{replacing }{Φ}_{0}(0)\text{ with }{I}_{n}\text{ in }x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c.$" :question/math-academy-id "q-337119" :question/problem "Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$  

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L6}$ by
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Line $\text{L5}$ gives

$$
({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c.
$$

Since $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}={I}_{n}$, the right-hand side simplifies to $c$, so

$$
c=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0}).
$$

Simplify once, then apply $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}$, to obtain

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L6}.$ Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L6}$, and $\text{L7}.$ From $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c.
$$

Using $\text{L6}$, we substitute $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})$ to obtain

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L7}.$ Thus, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L6}$ by $\text{substituting }c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\text{ into }x(t)={e}^{At}c.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can combine the exponentials:

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7}$ gives line $\text{L8}.$ Thus, line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{the fact that }{e}^{X}{e}^{Y}={e}^{X+Y}\text{ when }X\text{ and }Y\text{ commute}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9f300979-2c03-5bca-8541-1101107fdf73" [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351293 :question/worked-solution "First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](images/73/7316d667d7308ac5ec0f5348055d3d0e7eb90b97abaa74f5693c3151dc3b8bb1.png)

Now, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. 

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3-{x}^{2} & =x+1 \\ {x}^{2}+x-2 & =0 \\ (x-1)(x+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x$-limits are 
$-2\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/aa/aab6fb99694b518bfa9d200a75876c9e888ba1ab7d699464bc9caca360be775a.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 1,\,x+1\le y\le 3-{x}^{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}{\int }_{x+1}^{3-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}[{\int }_{x+1}^{3-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351295 :question/problem "Calculate ${∬}_{D}3x{e}^{y}\,dA,\,$
where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡x\}.$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over the type I region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡x\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3x{e}^{y}\,dA & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}3x{e}^{y}\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}3x{e}^{y}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{e}^{y}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x{[{e}^{y}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}-{e}^{0})dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x(x-1)dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(3{x}^{2}-3x)dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}(3{x}^{2}-3x)dx & ={[{x}^{3}-\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(64-24)-(1-\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =40+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{81}{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351369 :question/problem "Calculate ${∬}_{D}x\,dA,\,$
where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,2{x}^{2}\le y\le {x}^{2}+1\}.$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over the type I region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,2{x}^{2}\le y\le {x}^{2}+1\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}x\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}x\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x[{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x[y]_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x({x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(1-{x}^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{3})dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{3})dx & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-61556a8f-0a92-5ecd-8c20-5948347f1756" :question/id #uuid "61556a8f-0a92-5ecd-8c20-5948347f1756" :question/math-academy-id "q-132221" :question/problem "![](images/a6/a68077b18f8c08fc7cd68889b6472373c7677bcfcb6f370abce1e93cf67c4594.png)

If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the line $x=0,$ and the curves $y=5-{x}^{2}$ and $y=-\frac{1}{2}x,$ as shown above, then ${∬}_{D}x\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)\,dA=$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. 

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}x & =5-{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}x-5 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-x-10 & =0 \\ (x+2)(2x-5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We discard the solution $x=\frac{5}{2}$ since $x\le 0$ in our region. Therefore, $x$-limits are $-2\le x\le 0.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/5b/5bafe1d8cd35eec83aba3a9a24f777340a09f824919d4cedc5879c774e30cf5e.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 0,\,-\frac{1}{2}x\le y\le 5-{x}^{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)\,dA & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-x/2}^{5-{x}^{2}}x\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0dce35b7-572a-54b4-af44-152ecca7b2e8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

Now, we approximate the value of $\sqrt{2}$ using a calculator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} & ≈‭‭‭1.414\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186077888 :answer-field/correct 17592186077890 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186079667 :tutorial/content "Suppose we need to evaluate an expression like

$$
1+\sqrt{4},
$$

where we have a square root sign. What would be the order of operations? It turns out that the root signs ($\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$ or $\sqrt[3]{\phantom{x}}$) can be thought of as parentheses. 
In other words, we find the value under the square root first:

$$
\begin{aligned}1+\sqrt{4} & = \\ 1+2 & = \\ 3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Similarly, let's evaluate $\big(1-\sqrt[3]{-27}\big) \div 2$.

To evaluate expressions with radicals, we use PEMDAS as before, but with the following additional rules:

- expressions underneath radicals are treated the same as parentheses

- radicals themselves are treated as exponents

Following the order of operations, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(1-\sqrt[3]{-27})÷2 & = \\ (1-\sqrt[3]{(-3)^{3}})÷2 & = \\ (1-(-3))÷2 & = \\ 4÷2 & = \\ 2\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186079665 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to simplify the following expression:

$$
-3\sqrt{\left(2^4-1\right) \div 3}\,.
$$

The first thing to realize is that there is an invisible multiplication symbol here. The above expression is short for

$$
-3\,{\color{red}{\times}}\,\sqrt{\left(2^4-1\right) \div 3}\,.
$$

When multiplying a radical by a number, we usually omit the additional multiplication symbol.

Now, to simplify the given expression, we use PEMDAS.  In terms of the order of operations:

- Expressions underneath radicals are treated as if they are contained within parentheses (the **P** in **P**EMDAS), so we always deal with this first.

- Radicals themselves are treated as exponents (the **E** in P**E**MDAS).

Therefore, following PEMDAS, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-3\sqrt{({2}^{4}-1)÷3} & = \\ -3\sqrt{(16-1)÷3} & = \\ -3\sqrt{15÷3} & = \\ -3\sqrt{5} & .\end{aligned}
$$

And that's our answer! 

To get a numerical approximation, we need to use a calculator. In this case, we get

$$
-3 \sqrt{5} = -3\times \sqrt{5} \approx -6.708\,204
$$

rounded to six decimal places." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078630 :activity/expected-seconds 600.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186396437 :question/problem "The local truncation error (LTE) of a numerical method with step size $Δx$ is

$$
τ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}.
$$

Complete the following sentences.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Decreasing from $Δx=0.5$ to $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is reduced by a factor of $≈$
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ According to this data, the order of the method is approximately
{{field-4}}." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221404 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4b679574-cdae-5555-900f-72dfd634fac3"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-4b679574-cdae-5555-900f-72dfd634fac3" :question/id #uuid "4b679574-cdae-5555-900f-72dfd634fac3" :question/math-academy-id "q-334797" :question/problem "A numerical method for approximating a solution to an initial value problem is known to be order $3.$  Suppose that using step size $Δx=0.25$ produces a global truncation error (GTE) of $e(0.25)≈0.125.$  If we instead use a step size $Δx=0.10,$ what GTE should we expect?

$e(0.10)≈$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.25$ to $0.10.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.25}{0.10}=2.5.
$$

$$

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}{\color{blue}{a}} x + a^2 =  (x+{\color{blue}{a}})^2 .
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
x^2 + 12x + 36.
$$

First, we write the constant term as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+12x+{6}^{2} & \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of sum formula with ${\color{blue}{a}} = {\color{blue}{6}}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+6)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064326 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-380d2267-0a37-5388-bacc-f5df7afa8e5c" "question-94bbfbab-f0f9-56d8-b645-4168ecf299d7" "question-f18cf588-d703-5104-bc39-415b94a76959"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186063961 :question/problem "Factor $p^2 - 10p + 25.$" :question/worked-solution "The "square of a difference" formula states that

$$
p^2 - {\color{red}{2}}{\color{blue}{a}} p + a^2 =  (p-{\color{blue}{a}})^2 .
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
p^2 - 10p + 25.
$$

First, we write the constant term as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{2}-10p+{5}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{2}-2\cdot 5p+{5}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of difference formula with ${\color{blue}{a}} = {\color{blue}{5}}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-5)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064327 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3ab2e3ce-42ef-5550-a256-e8688e7ed48b" "question-33ad6f1c-10b4-54e8-b066-192c2a7ae636"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186063962 :question/problem "Factor the expression $y^2 + \dfrac{2}{5}y + \dfrac{1}{25}.$" :question/worked-solution "The "square of a sum" formula states that

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}{\color{blue}{a}} x + a^2 =  (x+{\color{blue}{a}})^2 .
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
y^2 + \dfrac{2}{5}y + \dfrac{1}{25}.
$$

First, we write the constant term as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+\frac{2}{5}y+{(\frac{1}{5})}^{2} & \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{5}y+{(\frac{1}{5})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of sum formula with ${\color{blue}{a}} = {\color{blue}{\dfrac 1 5}}.$ This gives

For example, the expression

$$
x^2 + 6x + 9
$$

is a perfect square trinomial because it is the result of squaring the binomial $(x+3)$, as shown below:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & = \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2} & = \\ {x}^{2}+6x+9 & \end{aligned}
$$

To factor a perfect square trinomial, we have to figure out what binomial it is the square of. We can often do this by relating the perfect square trinomial to the **square of a sum**:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}2}  {\color{blue}a}x + {\color{blue}a}^2 = (x + {\color{blue}a})^2
$$

 

To illustrate, let's factor the expression $x^2+6x+9$ using the square of sum formula. We perform the following steps:

1\. Write the constant term as a perfect square:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+{3}^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

2\. Factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

3\. Factor the trinomial using the "square of a sum formula". In this case, we have ${\color{blue}{a}}={\color{blue}{3}}\mathbin{:}$

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

This method works *only* when the trinomial is a perfect square! It will *not* work for every trinomial. We will learn more general methods in the future." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186065345 :tutorial/content "Other perfect square trinomials can be factored as the **square of a difference**:

$$
x^2 - {\color{red}2}  {\color{blue}a}x  + {\color{blue}a}^2 = (x - {\color{blue}a})^2
$$

 

To illustrate, let's factor the expression $x^2-10x+25$ using the square of difference formula. We perform the following steps:

1\. Write the constant term as a perfect square:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-10x+{5}^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

2\. Factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2\cdot 5x+{5}^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

3\. Factor the trinomial using the square of difference formula. In this case, we have ${\color{blue}{a}}={\color{blue}{5}},$ and we get

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(x-5)^{2}.\end{aligned}
  $$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064441 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068701 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-86c185f8-7069-5803-a8a3-6aebf9cf8dbc" "question-a662c339-4277-548c-aaa6-345c7b02ceaa"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068486 :question/problem "If $g(x) = (x-4)^2+3(5-x)$, calculate $g(2).$" :question/worked-solution "We substitute $x=2$ into the function definition and then simplify:

$$
\eqalign{
		g(x) &= (x-4)^2+3(5-x) \[5pt]
		g(2) &= (2-4)^2+3(5-2) \[5pt]
		      &= (-2)^2+3(3) \[5pt]
		      &= 4 + 9 \[5pt]
		      &= 13
	}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068702 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-9ddffbc5-a8dd-53fa-a3bc-4cc663a782e3" "question-377f9da3-7e91-540b-b15e-84984d6004ce"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068487 :question/problem "Evaluate $f(4,-1)$ if $f(x,y)= 3\cdot 2^{x+3y}.$" :question/worked-solution "We substitute $x=4$ and $y=-1$ into the function definition and then simplify:

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186066112 :answer-field/correct "answer-d8d28ec1-8bca-5b66-95e1-e3b9c1576a50" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d8d28ec1-8bca-5b66-95e1-e3b9c1576a50"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d8d28ec1-8bca-5b66-95e1-e3b9c1576a50" :answer/id #uuid "d8d28ec1-8bca-5b66-95e1-e3b9c1576a50" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186070022 :tutorial/content "A **function** is a rule that takes a number as **input** and then **outputs** another number.

For instance, let's look at the following function: 

$$
f(x) = 3x+1
$$

In this example,

- $f$ is the **name** of the function,

- the number $x$ is the **input**,

- the number $3x+1$ is the **output**.

If we **substitute** a number into our function in place of $x$, we get another number as output. 

For example, by substituting $x={\color{blue}{2}},$ we get

$$
f({\color{blue}{2}}) = 3\cdot {\color{blue}{2}}+1 = 7.
$$

So, the input $x={\color{blue}{2}}$ results in an output of $7.$

We can substitute any number we like into this function! For example, if we substitute $x={\color{red}{-2}},$ we get

$$
f({\color{red}{-2}}) = 3\cdot ({\color{red}{-2}})+1 = -5.
$$

So, the input $x={\color{red}{-2}}$ results in an output of $-5.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186070023 :tutorial/content "Functions with more than one input are called **multivariable functions**. 

For example, the multivariable function 

$$
f(x,y)=x-y
$$

takes in two numbers, $x$ and $y$, and returns their difference. 

For multivariable functions, the order of the inputs matters. For example, if we substitute $x={\color{blue}{3}}$ and $y={\color{red}{2}},$ we get

$$
f({\color{blue}{3}},{\color{red}{2}}) = {\color{blue}{3}}-{\color{red}{2}}=1,
$$

whereas if we substitute $x={\color{red}{2}}$ and $y={\color{blue}{3}},$ we get a different output:

$$
f({\color{red}{2}},{\color{blue}{3}})={\color{red}{2}}-{\color{blue}{3}}=-1
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068995 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176484 :question/problem "What is $(\sqrt{64})^{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "The number in the square root is non-negative, so the square and the square root cancel each other out.

![](images/a3/a3de8797a3b489ada861edbebb5de935dc5c840dafc509bf2b41ad093d7cc2b4.svg)" :question/worked-solution "The mode of a random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ is the value of $x$ at the global maximum of $f(x).$

To find the global maximum of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $0 \leq x\leq \pi$ is $f(x) = \dfrac{\sin x}{2}.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving $f'(x) = 0,$ we get

$$
\dfrac{\cos x}{2} = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad x= \dfrac{\pi}{2}+k\pi ,
$$

where $k$ is any integer.
Among these critical points, only $x= \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ lies within the interval $\left[0, \pi \right].$

- The derivative doesn't exist at the endpoints $x = 0, \pi.$ So, these are critical points as well.

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡0=0 \\ f(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{1}{2} \\ f(\pi ) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest value is

$$
f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the mode of $X$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162003 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-cc6f0c6d-fbfc-515f-9faf-cdb2e36bd29a" "question-3564d8be-ba15-5300-bf05-043e2a7c4f77" "question-04da65b8-370f-5d43-9d9a-986d048126c3" "question-fed1e82d-9029-565f-bbd7-a48e9974d84e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161795 :question/problem "Let $X$ be a random variable with the probability density function shown below. To find the global maxima of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $0 \leq x \leq 2$ is $f(x) = \dfrac{3}{2}(x-1)^2.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2(x-1) \\  & =3(x-1),\end{aligned}
$$

and solving $f'(x) = 0,$ we get

$$
3(x-1)= 0\quad \Longrightarrow \quad x=1.
$$

This critical point is within the interval $[0,2],$ so we keep it.

- The derivative doesn't exist at the endpoints $x = 0, 2.$ So, these are critical points as well.

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=0,1, 2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =\frac{3}{2}(0-1)^{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ f(1) & =\frac{3}{2}(1-1)^{2}=0 \\ f(2) & =\frac{3}{2}(2-1)^{2}=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest values are

$$
f(0 ) = f( 2) = \dfrac{3}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the modes of $X$ are $0$ and $2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-a5a77e1a-841f-57c5-8990-3f339cc0802e" :question/id #uuid "a5a77e1a-841f-57c5-8990-3f339cc0802e" :question/math-academy-id "q-95180" :question/problem "![](images/aa/aa2638a96ae91d0b2a8a0d1216e8256c7823c231c5ceecd9a4b3fd14c239ed53.png)

"d0fd2e28-4af0-53c5-9c68-348af97ab34c" :question/math-academy-id "q-95348" :question/problem "Let $X$ be a random variable with the probability density function shown below. What is the mode of $X?$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{100}(5+4x-{x}^{2}), & 0\le x\le 5 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The mode of a random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ is the value of $x$ at the global maximum of $f(x).$

To find the global maximum of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $0\le x\le 5$ is $f(x)=\frac{3}{100}(5+4x-{x}^{2}).$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{3}{100}(4-2x),\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get

$$
\frac{3}{100}(4-2x)=0\,⟹\,x=2.
$$

The point $x=2$ is in the interval $[0,5],$ so we keep it.

- The derivative doesn't exist at the endpoints $x=0,5.$ So, these are critical points as well.

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=0,2,5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =\frac{3}{100}(5+4\cdot 0-{0}^{2})=\frac{15}{100}=\frac{3}{20} \\ f(2) & =\frac{3}{100}(5+4\cdot 2-{2}^{2})=\frac{27}{100} \\ f(5) & =\frac{3}{100}(5+4\cdot 5-{5}^{2})=0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest value is

$$
f(2)=\frac{27}{100}
$$

What are the modes of $X?$

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "The modes of a random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ are the values of $x$ at the global maxima of $f(x).$

To find the global maxima of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $-2\le x\le 2$ is $f(x)=\frac{(2-x)(x+1)^{2}}{8}.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{-(x+1)^{2}+2(2-x)(x+1)}{8} \\  & =\frac{(x+1)(-x-1+4-2x)}{8} \\  & =\frac{3(x+1)(1-x)}{8},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get

$$
\frac{3(x+1)(1-x)}{8}\,⟹\,x=-1,1.
$$

All of these critical points are within the interval $[-2,2],$ so we keep them all.

- The derivative doesn't exist at the endpoints $x=-2,2.$ So, these are critical points as well.

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=-2,-1,1,2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-2) & =\frac{(2+2)(-2+1)^{2}}{8}=\frac{1}{2} \\ f(-1) & =\frac{(2+1)(-1+1)^{2}}{8}=0 \\ f(1) & =\frac{(2-1)(1+1)^{2}}{8}=\frac{1}{2} \\ f(2) & =\frac{(2-2)(2+1)^{2}}{8}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest values are

$$
f(-2)=f(1)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the modes of $X$ are $-2$ and $1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-89711e9c-e116-50a7-ae9d-6fbf9295b7f8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-89711e9c-e116-50a7-ae9d-6fbf9295b7f8" :answer-field/id #uuid "89711e9c-e116-50a7-ae9d-6fbf9295b7f8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-803b79a6-bd27-5019-a0ca-6c717c883e01" :answer-field/choices ["answer-616aa6a5-4b43-534d-821a-bbdbc35c16f3" "answer-8002f0e0-b8eb-52ab-98a1-fb52f05547d2" "answer-d675c4d0-7a79-5251-b122-3bcefc69e692" "answer-803b79a6-bd27-5019-a0ca-6c717c883e01" "answer-91229bac-46a3-5f6c-aba9-119cb3512ae8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-616aa6a5-4b43-534d-821a-bbdbc35c16f3" :answer/id #uuid "616aa6a5-4b43-534d-821a-bbdbc35c16f3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1,1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8002f0e0-b8eb-52ab-98a1-fb52f05547d2" :answer/id #uuid "8002f0e0-b8eb-52ab-98a1-fb52f05547d2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1,1,2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d675c4d0-7a79-5251-b122-3bcefc69e692" :answer/id #uuid "d675c4d0-7a79-5251-b122-3bcefc69e692" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2,-1,1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-803b79a6-bd27-5019-a0ca-6c717c883e01" :answer/id #uuid "803b79a6-bd27-5019-a0ca-6c717c883e01" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2,1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-91229bac-46a3-5f6c-aba9-119cb3512ae8" :answer/id #uuid "91229bac-46a3-5f6c-aba9-119cb3512ae8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2,2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-04da65b8-370f-5d43-9d9a-986d048126c3" :question/id #uuid "04da65b8-370f-5d43-9d9a-986d048126c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-97023" :question/problem "Let $X$ be a random variable with the probability density function shown below. $$" :question/worked-solution "The modes of a random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ are the values of $x$ at the global maxima of $f(x).$

To find the global maxima of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $0\le x\le 8$ is $f(x)=\frac{x(6-x)^{2}}{128}.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{(6-x)^{2}-2x(6-x)}{128} \\  & =\frac{(6-x)(6-x-2x)}{128} \\  & =\frac{3(6-x)(2-x)}{128},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get

$$
\frac{3(6-x)(2-x)}{128}\,⟹\,x=2,6.
$$

All of these critical points are within the interval $[0,8],$ so we keep them all.

- The derivative doesn't exist at the endpoints $x=0,8.$ So, these are critical points as well.

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=0,2,6,8:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =\frac{0(6-0)^{2}}{128}=0 \\ f(2) & =\frac{2(6-2)^{2}}{128}=\frac{1}{4} \\ f(6) & =\frac{6(6-6)^{2}}{128}=0 \\ f(8) & =\frac{8(6-8)^{2}}{128}=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest values are

$$
f(2)=f(8)=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the modes of $X$ are $2$ and $8.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f864eeb7-5c3a-520c-b5c5-87f43508e40a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f864eeb7-5c3a-520c-b5c5-87f43508e40a" :answer-field/id #uuid "f864eeb7-5c3a-520c-b5c5-87f43508e40a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-c956b69f-1371-5064-85a7-92f548f1708c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2a39c9ca-304c-5dc6-bf0a-a3191df9d199" "answer-2fc1d53b-065c-5f28-baee-103cc2d04fe5" "answer-6c32fa51-116b-5e6b-8ad8-9c15a7a0762b" "answer-25cf873b-c561-529e-a150-dbd67081b794" "answer-c956b69f-1371-5064-85a7-92f548f1708c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2a39c9ca-304c-5dc6-bf0a-a3191df9d199" :answer/id #uuid "2a39c9ca-304c-5dc6-bf0a-a3191df9d199" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0,2,6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2fc1d53b-065c-5f28-baee-103cc2d04fe5" :answer/id #uuid "2fc1d53b-065c-5f28-baee-103cc2d04fe5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0,2,8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6c32fa51-116b-5e6b-8ad8-9c15a7a0762b" :answer/id #uuid "6c32fa51-116b-5e6b-8ad8-9c15a7a0762b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2,6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-25cf873b-c561-529e-a150-dbd67081b794" :answer/id #uuid "25cf873b-c561-529e-a150-dbd67081b794" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2,6,8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c956b69f-1371-5064-85a7-92f548f1708c" :answer/id #uuid "c956b69f-1371-5064-85a7-92f548f1708c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2,8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-fed1e82d-9029-565f-bbd7-a48e9974d84e" :question/id #uuid "fed1e82d-9029-565f-bbd7-a48e9974d84e" :question/math-academy-id "q-127090" :question/problem "Let $X$ be a random variable with the probability density function shown below. What are the modes of $X?$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{96}{595}({x}^{4}-2{x}^{2}-2), & -1\le x\le \frac{3}{2} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The modes of a random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ are the values of $x$ at the global maxima of $f(x).$

To find the global maxima of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $-1\le x\le \frac{3}{2}$ is $f(x)=-\frac{96}{595}({x}^{4}-2{x}^{2}-2).$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{96}{595}(4{x}^{3}-4x) \\  & =-\frac{384}{595}x({x}^{2}-1),\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get

$$
-\frac{384}{595}x({x}^{2}-1)=0\,⟹\,x=0,\pm 1.
$$

All of these critical points are within the interval $[-1,\frac{3}{2}],$ so we keep them all.

- The derivative doesn't exist at the endpoints $x=\pm 1.$ So, these are critical points as well, but $-1$ is included above.

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=0,\pm 1,\frac{3}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1) & =-\frac{96}{595}((-1)^{4}-2(-1)^{2}-2)=\frac{288}{595} \\ f(0) & =-\frac{96}{595}((0)^{4}-2(0)^{2}-2)=\frac{192}{595} \\ f(1) & =-\frac{96}{595}((1)^{4}-2(1)^{2}-2)=\frac{288}{595} \\ f(\frac{3}{2}) & =-\frac{96}{595}({(\frac{3}{2})}^{4}-2{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-2)=\frac{138}{595}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest values are

$$
f(-1)=f(1)=\frac{288}{595}.
$$

Therefore, the modes of $X$ are $-1$ and $1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-68323756-6915-5a2a-b83f-b1d14e9cdd18"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-68323756-6915-5a2a-b83f-b1d14e9cdd18" :answer-field/id #uuid "68323756-6915-5a2a-b83f-b1d14e9cdd18" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1a3281f8-9551-52d3-8d0c-c6b89b2d2548" :answer-field/choices ["answer-16ac1ac8-5d12-5b50-934c-de82720f574b" "answer-4dde1e24-43fb-5f71-b240-852e369c1dd1" "answer-1a3281f8-9551-52d3-8d0c-c6b89b2d2548" "answer-c0cdcb5b-73ea-5836-bf70-b1a7b83f23d3" "answer-22e163e2-c51b-5f8c-acce-093bdea2aa79"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-16ac1ac8-5d12-5b50-934c-de82720f574b" :answer/id #uuid "16ac1ac8-5d12-5b50-934c-de82720f574b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1,0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4dde1e24-43fb-5f71-b240-852e369c1dd1" :answer/id #uuid "4dde1e24-43fb-5f71-b240-852e369c1dd1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1,0,1,\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1a3281f8-9551-52d3-8d0c-c6b89b2d2548" :answer/id #uuid "1a3281f8-9551-52d3-8d0c-c6b89b2d2548" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1,1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c0cdcb5b-73ea-5836-bf70-b1a7b83f23d3" :answer/id #uuid "c0cdcb5b-73ea-5836-bf70-b1a7b83f23d3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1,\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-22e163e2-c51b-5f8c-acce-093bdea2aa79" :answer/id #uuid "22e163e2-c51b-5f8c-acce-093bdea2aa79" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0,1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163240 :tutorial/content "The **modes of a random variable $X$** with probability density function $f(x)$ are the values of $x$ at the global maxima of $f(x).$

For example, the modes of the random variable $X$ with the probability density function shown below are ${\color{blue}5}$ and ${\color{blue}9}$ (the values of $x$ that correspond to the global maxima):

![](images/49/49e3f3c63c01ce5c00e9d2ff51bcd03d7516f7866f510ce091071a13a8496210.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163259 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose we are given the random variable $X$ with the probability density function shown below. 

![](images/ec/ec48a5d839f3d843fe4738707ec3d067a19db9b009f4bf29673d899b321248a3.svg)

How can we find the mode of $X$ algebraically? 

To find the global maximum of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $0 \leq x \leq 1$ is $f(x) =2x.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, there are no solutions  of  $f'(x) = 0.$

- The derivative doesn't exist at the endpoints $x = 0,1.$ So, these are critical points.

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=0,1{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =2(0)=0 \\ f(1) & =2(1)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest value is

$$
f({\color{blue}1}) =2.
$$

Therefore, the mode of $X$ is ${\color{blue}1}.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162179 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133800 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e65b2b16-1d73-53d7-b99e-0f6611b54099" "question-72a8e42a-c396-5007-82f3-4a7623931a98" "question-22478d60-239d-58ef-b70b-d84ab0dcc7e7"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133799 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f16e5a65-b3a9-5e9e-afd2-4d31b6ccc499"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133608 :question/problem "Find the least-squares solution to the system of linear equations given below. $$

We can find the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$

$$

Given that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, find the minimum value of $‖Ax-b‖.$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 9 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "First of all, we write the given system in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]}}\overset{x}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 9 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\ Ax & =b\end{aligned}
$$

We can find the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,\,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 9 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}16 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}16 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}A\overset{^}{x}-b & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 9 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
‖A\overset{^}{x}-b‖=\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(-4)^{2}}=\sqrt{35}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-791b26ae-4f7f-58a8-b298-28b8f970263b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-791b26ae-4f7f-58a8-b298-28b8f970263b" :answer-field/id #uuid "791b26ae-4f7f-58a8-b298-28b8f970263b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-164af3d4-d329-5a63-9544-443eea1cc4f5" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8eaa36ae-b43e-5ed4-8193-ae54fff3942f" "answer-e5ce1773-5c8b-5827-b29e-4b8dba8f0126" "answer-164af3d4-d329-5a63-9544-443eea1cc4f5" "answer-2daf4fd5-f4c3-5cde-bed6-b74154aa47b7" "answer-2bbf719c-8336-5b63-8170-1187e7f4e55b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8eaa36ae-b43e-5ed4-8193-ae54fff3942f" :answer/id #uuid "8eaa36ae-b43e-5ed4-8193-ae54fff3942f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\sqrt{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e5ce1773-5c8b-5827-b29e-4b8dba8f0126" :answer/id #uuid "e5ce1773-5c8b-5827-b29e-4b8dba8f0126" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5\sqrt{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-164af3d4-d329-5a63-9544-443eea1cc4f5" :answer/id #uuid "164af3d4-d329-5a63-9544-443eea1cc4f5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{35}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2daf4fd5-f4c3-5cde-bed6-b74154aa47b7" :answer/id #uuid "2daf4fd5-f4c3-5cde-bed6-b74154aa47b7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2bbf719c-8336-5b63-8170-1187e7f4e55b" :answer/id #uuid "2bbf719c-8336-5b63-8170-1187e7f4e55b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135059 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-2 \\ -{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=4 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

It is easy to show that the system is inconsistent (i.e., it has no solution). However, in real-world problems, we might want to find an approximate solution to the system. 

Let's formulate the problem a little more rigorously. Firstly, we write down the system in the form $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b\mathbin{:}$
![](images/22/22b8abd4638e579875755f482442cf1dbf89653bd9d396b4a802217e25177839.svg)

We are interested in vectors $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ such that $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is very close to $\mathbf b.$ More precisely, we wish to *minimize the distance* between $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and $\mathbf b.$ Recall that the distance between $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and $\mathbf b$ is given by

$$
\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert.
$$

The smaller the value of $\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert,$ the better our approximation $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ will be. 

In terms of vector subspaces, we wish to find a vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ that lies in $\textrm{Col}(A)$ and is closest to $\mathbf{b}.$
Therefore, $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ must be the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$

![](images/3a/3a1c79036954f0e04212892b7e3d79c75f8cd7b81d7785441f090f89a4eb6faf.png)

It can be shown that ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is found by solving the corresponding **normal equation**, given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

We'll prove this at the end of the lesson. Note that the normal equation is obtained by left-multiplying the equation $A {\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = \mathbf b$ by $A^T.$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix $A^T \! A$ is invertible. Therefore, left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T \! A)^{-1},$ we obtain

$$
{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = (A^T \! A)^{-1}A^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

We now compute the right-hand side as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -4 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,\,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 18\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{99}[\begin{aligned}18 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{33} \\ -\frac{38}{33}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is called the **least-squares solution** of the given system.

**Watch out!** We assumed that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, which guarantees that $A^T \! A\,$ is invertible. $$

$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}

$$

Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $6$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 6,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =((\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2})\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{6}{\rho }^{5}{sin}^{3}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cc1dcc32-b424-50ae-8bc7-6bf9e3e11130"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})^{3}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\sqrt{{({\rho }^{2})}^{3}} \\  & ={\rho }^{3}\end{aligned}

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=-16y$ for $x\le 0$ and $z\ge 0,$ shown above. 
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$  represents one-quarter of the sphere of radius $8$ centered at $(0,-8,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=-16y$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =-16y \\ {\rho }^{2} & =-16\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho +16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =-16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](images/86/868214a1c2b30da5b16b7f0c307b369bdc9f2d2201ee0ad5a3f5da2a8bdc6f49.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le -16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\pi \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\sqrt{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{-16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3d8e45e3-b187-55ef-8895-829cbde8baad"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=-2x,$ shown above. 
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $1$ centered at $(-1,0,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=-2x$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =-2x \\ {\rho }^{2} & =-2\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](images/43/43e3c386086d30431405bb3fe2ca2835595641041dd7e098f9234cab8e7b225d.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{1}{{\rho }^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{{\rho }^{2}}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-470c2112-2e6b-5e03-b248-67e3dc557d2a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128047 :answer-field/correct "answer-2ba2f8bc-07b7-555b-abce-2dbd526387b8" :answer-field/choices ["answer-70c5bbdd-a425-59db-9485-4faa31a3b688" "answer-77a30a35-8585-5967-8315-37366fe40e4e" "answer-2ba2f8bc-07b7-555b-abce-2dbd526387b8" "answer-8f37f742-d997-54de-b9c5-8167d0c0fb92" "answer-ccae1240-5ff0-5901-882e-959174fe23e9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-70c5bbdd-a425-59db-9485-4faa31a3b688" :answer/id #uuid "70c5bbdd-a425-59db-9485-4faa31a3b688" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\pi \sqrt{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-77a30a35-8585-5967-8315-37366fe40e4e" :answer/id #uuid "77a30a35-8585-5967-8315-37366fe40e4e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\pi \sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2ba2f8bc-07b7-555b-abce-2dbd526387b8" :answer/id #uuid "2ba2f8bc-07b7-555b-abce-2dbd526387b8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8f37f742-d997-54de-b9c5-8167d0c0fb92" :answer/id #uuid "8f37f742-d997-54de-b9c5-8167d0c0fb92" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{12}{\pi }" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ccae1240-5ff0-5901-882e-959174fe23e9" :answer/id #uuid "ccae1240-5ff0-5901-882e-959174fe23e9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{{\pi }^{2}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0136e908-03ab-5353-9218-7031e36c58ca" :question/id #uuid "0136e908-03ab-5353-9218-7031e36c58ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-161787" :question/problem "![](images/61/61bd212879bc2f37dba7637bb3b126e33c5f7b0fbebd5a676874d9b3f6bc38da.png)

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $3$ centered at $(0,3,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=6y$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =6y \\ {\rho }^{2} & =6\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](images/f5/f52fe1c2e73dcbe972d72d263a5a43f2c99dbd573395fbf6e3a3b78b46e1f461.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{1}{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{1}{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}[\rho ]_{\rho =0}^{\rho =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ-0)\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi }dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,d\theta  \\  & =6[ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =6(\pi -0)\cdot (-0+1) \\  & =6\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-453a80d3-4572-568f-a182-685985b15243"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-453a80d3-4572-568f-a182-685985b15243" :answer-field/id #uuid "453a80d3-4572-568f-a182-685985b15243" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-109a83cd-781d-5694-9781-188bd9aaeeb3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4a6483cc-ffc1-5e9c-84c3-e71f0a0fde29" "answer-89405e80-2f4a-52b4-8de1-3252e9336dd9" "answer-109a83cd-781d-5694-9781-188bd9aaeeb3" "answer-50912d13-7637-55d7-a096-19d196f870ed" "answer-127f15fb-77a4-5f53-a36b-526f40d40b1b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4a6483cc-ffc1-5e9c-84c3-e71f0a0fde29" :answer/id #uuid "4a6483cc-ffc1-5e9c-84c3-e71f0a0fde29" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-89405e80-2f4a-52b4-8de1-3252e9336dd9" :answer/id #uuid "89405e80-2f4a-52b4-8de1-3252e9336dd9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-109a83cd-781d-5694-9781-188bd9aaeeb3" :answer/id #uuid "109a83cd-781d-5694-9781-188bd9aaeeb3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-50912d13-7637-55d7-a096-19d196f870ed" :answer/id #uuid "50912d13-7637-55d7-a096-19d196f870ed" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-127f15fb-77a4-5f53-a36b-526f40d40b1b" :answer/id #uuid "127f15fb-77a4-5f53-a36b-526f40d40b1b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186371961 :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{\rho }\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{[\frac{1}{2}{\rho }^{2}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =4\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta  \\  & =8{[-\frac{1}{3}{cos}^{3}⁡ϕ]}_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi /2}\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}(0-1)\cdot (2\pi -0) \\  & =\frac{16\pi }{3}\end{aligned}

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-quarter of the sphere of radius $1$ centered at the origin.

![](images/ec/ec2f6c67eee7f836cc71efec2b17c2276aa8a9d397c632b3c499a46a75f7b95c.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 1,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{6}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\rho }^{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{\rho }^{8}\,d\rho  \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi /2}\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =-\pi /2}^{\theta =\pi /2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{9}{\rho }^{9}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =1} \\  & =-(0-1)\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}-(-\frac{\pi }{2}))\cdot \frac{1}{9}(1-0) \\  & =1\cdot \pi \cdot \frac{1}{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{9}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-748331ec-5745-5dc8-9854-65c69f6cb19e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-748331ec-5745-5dc8-9854-65c69f6cb19e" :answer-field/id #uuid "748331ec-5745-5dc8-9854-65c69f6cb19e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1508999f-583d-5409-a945-a2774f7b6030" :answer-field/choices ["answer-fdb401e4-0e59-57f0-b798-ca38f29d946f" "answer-1e78963c-6d08-52e4-886b-c299ac1eab3b" "answer-a5dfe954-7d04-5a12-8506-1f9267e2a525" "answer-1508999f-583d-5409-a945-a2774f7b6030" "answer-107bc90b-168a-5ae7-9c1e-5151de594035"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fdb401e4-0e59-57f0-b798-ca38f29d946f" :answer/id #uuid "fdb401e4-0e59-57f0-b798-ca38f29d946f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1e78963c-6d08-52e4-886b-c299ac1eab3b" :answer/id #uuid "1e78963c-6d08-52e4-886b-c299ac1eab3b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a5dfe954-7d04-5a12-8506-1f9267e2a525" :answer/id #uuid "a5dfe954-7d04-5a12-8506-1f9267e2a525" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5\pi }{8}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1508999f-583d-5409-a945-a2774f7b6030" :answer/id #uuid "1508999f-583d-5409-a945-a2774f7b6030" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{9}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-107bc90b-168a-5ae7-9c1e-5151de594035" :answer/id #uuid "107bc90b-168a-5ae7-9c1e-5151de594035" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130455 :tutorial/content "When evaluating triple integrals, it's sometimes easier to change the variables from Cartesian coordinates to spherical polar coordinates.

For example, suppose we want to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R \left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2\right)^{3/2} \: \textrm{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the region enclosed by the sphere of radius $1$ centered at $O,$ as shown below.

![](images/08/0809a74f0aca2b3042b7f8db6783f9d6a13bc84bfc75ddcbb4d3076dbf0a2efd.png)

This integral seems too challenging when written in Cartesian coordinates. However, we should recognize that the problem lends itself to spherical polar coordinates because

- the domain $R$ has a simple spherical polar representation, and

- the integrand $f(x,y,z)=\left(x^2+y^2+z^2\right)^{3/2}$ can also be expressed simply in spherical polar coordinates.

So, let's transform the entire problem to spherical polar coordinates using the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined by

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad

y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 

z = \rho\cos\phi.
$$

The preimage of $R$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the rectangular region $\Delta,$ given by

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (\rho, \theta, \phi) \, : \, 0 \leq \rho \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: 0 \leq \phi \leq \pi \right\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/c2/c2ed8a57c5e66687428a524eb148f96672f3a1ace7fbd28d426de065b2fb5f1f.png)

To express our integral in terms of spherical polar coordinates, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 

\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi.
$$

It can be shown that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant for a spherical change of variables is

$$
\left| \dfrac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2\sin\phi.
$$

Therefore, the change of variables formula is

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 

\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \:  \rho^2\sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi.
$$

Now, let's write our function $f(x,y,z) = \left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2\right)^{3/2}$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & ={({\rho }^{2})}^{3/2} \\  & ={\rho }^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{3}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\rho }^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{\rho }^{5}\,d\rho  \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{6}{\rho }^{6}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =1}\,d\rho  \\  & =-(-1-1)\cdot (2\pi -0)\cdot \frac{1}{6}(1-0) \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130468 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've used the fact that 

$$
\left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2 \sin{\phi}.
$$

Let's now prove this result.

Given the spherical coordinate transformations

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad

y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 

z = \rho\cos\phi,
$$

we first  calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂x}{∂\theta } & =-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂x}{∂ϕ} & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \frac{∂y}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta } & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂y}{∂ϕ} & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \frac{∂z}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta } & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂ϕ} & =-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & -\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & 0 & -\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ|\begin{aligned}-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}|-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & -\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\cdot (-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ))-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \rho {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ \\  & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) \\  & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
\left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2 \sin{\phi}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130469 :tutorial/content "We can also derive the change of variables formula for spherical polar coordinates using geometry.

Consider a bounded spherical box $R,$ given by

$$
R = \big\{ (\rho,\theta,\phi) \: | \: a \leq \rho \leq b, \:\: \alpha \leq \theta \leq \beta, \:\: \gamma \leq \phi \leq \psi \big\}.
$$

We can divide each interval into $l,m,$ and $n$ subdivisions such that 

$$
\Delta\rho = \dfrac{b-a}{l},\qquad \Delta\theta = \dfrac{\beta-\alpha}{m},\qquad \Delta\phi = \dfrac{\psi-\gamma}{n}.
$$

This splits the region into "spherical wedges," as shown in the following diagram.

![](images/88/88be4c6a09062321d20ac7f48dfbb6be796cdd6b5bb1b7f6adc49a6ae1da609b.png)

Zooming in on one of these wedges, we obtain a shape resembling a rectangular solid.

![](images/5e/5e5f7acb4d057e856c66e9d5626f81178ca26c0b7ce83cdf7290b1f4c64b1852.png)

Let's note the volume of this solid as $\Delta V.$ To approximate the value of $\Delta V,$ we use the formula for the volume of a rectangular solid:

$$
\Delta V \approx lwh
$$

Clearly, the height of the rectangular solid is $h = \Delta \rho.$ We can find the remaining dimensions using simple geometry. 

First, we need to find the length of the radius $r$ in the $xy$-plane. Using the following triangle and a side-on view of the wedge, we conclude that $r=\rho\sin\phi.$

![](images/01/0122c6c3b813bbe2821dbede794b6027cd69002dd1828925811211045a0d67e8.png)

Let's add this to our diagram.

![](images/d4/d41b538e9bb3add9bae1e3a24c9f87ae282a8b969f0c0dc4acd374ad777de74a.png)

Finally, we can use the arc length formula $s = r \cdot \theta$ to find the length $l$ and width $w.$

![](images/88/882b9243d1189c098aaf6e1e45ca7ec97d480b1f2c3a8fe23d5e39a6c2313ed2.png)

The length of our wedge is 

$$
l = \rho \cdot \Delta\phi = \rho\Delta\phi
$$

 and the width is 

$$
w = \rho\sin\phi \cdot \Delta\theta = \rho\sin\phi\Delta\theta.
$$

Calculating the volume as a rectangular solid, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}ΔV & ≈lwh \\  & =(\rho Δϕ)\cdot (\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕΔ\theta )\cdot (Δ\rho ) \\  & ={\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,Δϕ\,Δ\theta \,Δ\rho .\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we define the triple integral in spherical coordinates as the limit of a triple Riemann sum, where $(\rho_{ijk},\theta_{ijk},\phi_{ijk})$ being any sample point in the spherical subregion $B{ijk}{:}$

$$
\lim\limits_{l,m,n \to \infty} \sum\limits_{i=1}^{l} \sum\limits_{j=1}^{m} \sum\limits_{k=1}^{n} f(\rho_{ijk},\theta_{ijk},\phi_{ijk}) (\rho_{ijk})^2 \sin \phi_{ijk} \:\Delta\rho\:\Delta\theta\:\Delta\phi
$$

As we increase the number of subregions, the size of $\Delta\rho,$ $\Delta\theta,$ and $\Delta\phi$ all goes to zero, and the volume of $R$ is more accurately approximated, giving

$$
\textrm{d}V = \rho^2 \sin\phi \:\textrm{d}\rho\:\textrm{d}\theta\:\textrm{d}\phi.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that if $f(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ is continuous on a spherical box $R = [a,b] \times [\alpha,\beta] \times [\gamma, \psi],$ then

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(\rho,\theta,\phi) \:\textrm{d}V
=
\iiint\limits_{R} f(\rho,\theta,\phi) \rho^2 \sin\phi \:\textrm{d}\rho\:\textrm{d}\theta\:\textrm{d}\phi
=
\int_{\gamma}^{\psi}\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\int_{a}^{b} f(\rho,\theta,\phi) \rho^2 \sin\phi \:\textrm{d}\rho\:\textrm{d}\theta\:\textrm{d}\phi.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129390 :activity/expected-seconds 1200.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

which of the following could be the definition of $f(x,y)?$

I. $\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y, & (x,y)\in D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D\end{aligned}$

II. $\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y, & (x,y)\in R\cap D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D\end{aligned}$

III. $\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y, & (x,y)\in R∖D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in D\end{aligned}$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's draw our region $D$ and rectangle $R:$

![](images/1c/1ca0b430b798a6dc85fd2b731a93690f79bb2c45b33bbe6f31a5618a2ce0888a.png)

Notice that the rectangle $R$ contains the region $D$ completely. 

Now, if we define $f(x,y)$ to be equal $\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ on $D$ and to be equal $0$ outside $D,$ we obtain

$$
{∬}_{D}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given functions.
