To find the global maxima of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $-2\le x\le 2$ is $f(x)=\frac{(2-x)(x+1)^{2}}{8}.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get

$$
\frac{3(x+1)(1-x)}{8}\,⟹\,x=-1,1.
$$

All of these critical points are within the interval $[-2,2],$ so we keep them all.

- The derivative doesn't exist at the endpoints $x=-2,2.$ So, these are critical points as well.

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=-2,-1,1,2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-2) & =\frac{(2+2)(-2+1)^{2}}{8}=\frac{1}{2} \\ f(-1) & =\frac{(2+1)(-1+1)^{2}}{8}=0 \\ f(1) & =\frac{(2-1)(1+1)^{2}}{8}=\frac{1}{2} \\ f(2) & =\frac{(2-2)(2+1)^{2}}{8}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest values are

$$
f(-2)=f(1)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

What are the modes of $X?$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{x(6-x)^{2}}{128}, & 0\le x\le 8 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-04da65b8-370f-5d43-9d9a-986d048126c3" :question/worked-solution "The modes of a random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ are the values of $x$ at the global maxima of $f(x).$

To find the global maxima of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $0\le x\le 8$ is $f(x)=\frac{x(6-x)^{2}}{128}.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{(6-x)^{2}-2x(6-x)}{128} \\  & =\frac{(6-x)(6-x-2x)}{128} \\  & =\frac{3(6-x)(2-x)}{128},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get

$$
\frac{3(6-x)(2-x)}{128}\,⟹\,x=2,6.
$$

All of these critical points are within the interval $[0,8],$ so we keep them all.

- The derivative doesn't exist at the endpoints $x=0,8.$ So, these are critical points as well.

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=0,2,6,8:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =\frac{0(6-0)^{2}}{128}=0 \\ f(2) & =\frac{2(6-2)^{2}}{128}=\frac{1}{4} \\ f(6) & =\frac{6(6-6)^{2}}{128}=0 \\ f(8) & =\frac{8(6-8)^{2}}{128}=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest values are

$$
f(2)=f(8)=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the modes of $X$ are $2$ and $8.$"] ["question-04da65b8-370f-5d43-9d9a-986d048126c3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-f864eeb7-5c3a-520c-b5c5-87f43508e40a" $$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{96}{595}({x}^{4}-2{x}^{2}-2), & -1\le x\le \frac{3}{2} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-fed1e82d-9029-565f-bbd7-a48e9974d84e" :question/worked-solution "The modes of a random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ are the values of $x$ at the global maxima of $f(x).$

To find the global maxima of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $-1\le x\le \frac{3}{2}$ is $f(x)=-\frac{96}{595}({x}^{4}-2{x}^{2}-2).$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{96}{595}(4{x}^{3}-4x) \\  & =-\frac{384}{595}x({x}^{2}-1),\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get

$$
-\frac{384}{595}x({x}^{2}-1)=0\,⟹\,x=0,\pm 1.
$$

All of these critical points are within the interval $[-1,\frac{3}{2}],$ so we keep them all.

- The derivative doesn't exist at the endpoints $x=\pm 1.$ So, these are critical points as well, but $-1$ is included above.

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=0,\pm 1,\frac{3}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1) & =-\frac{96}{595}((-1)^{4}-2(-1)^{2}-2)=\frac{288}{595} \\ f(0) & =-\frac{96}{595}((0)^{4}-2(0)^{2}-2)=\frac{192}{595} \\ f(1) & =-\frac{96}{595}((1)^{4}-2(1)^{2}-2)=\frac{288}{595} \\ f(\frac{3}{2}) & =-\frac{96}{595}({(\frac{3}{2})}^{4}-2{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-2)=\frac{138}{595}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest values are

$$
f(-1)=f(1)=\frac{288}{595}.
$$

Therefore, the modes of $X$ are $-1$ and $1.$"] ["question-fed1e82d-9029-565f-bbd7-a48e9974d84e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-68323756-6915-5a2a-b83f-b1d14e9cdd18" $\,$ $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$"] ["question-e65b2b16-1d73-53d7-b99e-0f6611b54099" :question/worked-solution "First of all, we write the given system in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\overset{x}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}}
$$

We can find the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{18}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{18}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e65b2b16-1d73-53d7-b99e-0f6611b54099" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-46985715-006b-561e-9632-119e4caaef8f" :answer-field/id #uuid A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 9 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$"] ["question-bbdebe64-e032-577f-8298-161c9dc3fe78" :question/worked-solution "First of all, we write the given system in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]}}\overset{x}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 9 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\ Ax & =b\end{aligned}
$$

We can find the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,\,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 9 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}16 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}16 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The minimum value of $‖Ax-b‖$ is attained when $x=\overset{^}{x},$ which is the least-squares solution of the system $Ax=b.$ In this case, $A\overset{^}{x}$ represents the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto the column space of $A,$ and $‖A\overset{^}{x}-b‖$ is the distance between the vector $b$ and the column space. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}A\overset{^}{x}-b & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 9 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
‖A\overset{^}{x}-b‖=\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(-4)^{2}}=\sqrt{35}.
$$"] ["question-bbdebe64-e032-577f-8298-161c9dc3fe78" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-791b26ae-4f7f-58a8-b298-28b8f970263b" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-bbdebe64-e032-577f-8298-161c9dc3fe78"] [17592186135059 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-2 \\ -{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=4 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

It is easy to show that the system is inconsistent (i.e., it has no solution). However, in real-world problems, we might want to find an approximate solution to the system. 

Let's formulate the problem a little more rigorously. Firstly, we write down the system in the form $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b\mathbin{:}$
![](images/22/22b8abd4638e579875755f482442cf1dbf89653bd9d396b4a802217e25177839.svg)

We are interested in vectors $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ such that $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is very close to $\mathbf b.$ More precisely, we wish to *minimize the distance* between $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and $\mathbf b.$ Recall that the distance between $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and $\mathbf b$ is given by

$$
\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert.
$$

The smaller the value of $\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert,$ the better our approximation $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ will be. 

In terms of vector subspaces, we wish to find a vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ that lies in $\textrm{Col}(A)$ and is closest to $\mathbf{b}.$
Therefore, $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ must be the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$

![](images/3a/3a1c79036954f0e04212892b7e3d79c75f8cd7b81d7785441f090f89a4eb6faf.png)

It can be shown that ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is found by solving the corresponding **normal equation**, given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

We'll prove this at the end of the lesson. Note that the normal equation is obtained by left-multiplying the equation $A {\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = \mathbf b$ by $A^T.$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix $A^T \! A$ is invertible. Therefore, left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T \! A)^{-1},$ we obtain

$$
{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = (A^T \! A)^{-1}A^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

We now compute the right-hand side as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -4 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,\,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 18\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{99}[\begin{aligned}18 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{33} \\ -\frac{38}{33}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is called the **least-squares solution** of the given system.

**Watch out!** We assumed that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, which guarantees that $A^T \! A\,$ is invertible. However, if the columns of $A$ are linearly *dependent,* then we have to use a different approach to solve the problem."] ["question-ac302ee6-6bbe-5388-bf60-4247113c7536" :question/id #uuid "ac302ee6-6bbe-5388-bf60-4247113c7536"] ["question-ac302ee6-6bbe-5388-bf60-4247113c7536" :question/math-academy-id "q-161750"] ["question-ac302ee6-6bbe-5388-bf60-4247113c7536" :question/problem "The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$"] ["question-ac302ee6-6bbe-5388-bf60-4247113c7536" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le \sqrt{2},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}{\rho }^{5}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{3}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ac302ee6-6bbe-5388-bf60-4247113c7536" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-a40abc4f-2947-5476-abce-6432706d5eb5" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}xz({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}V
$$"] ["question-31ed4558-6b89-5259-81f7-c1113b514f8f" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le \frac{1}{2},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=xz({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2} \\  & ={\rho }^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}xz({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{\rho }^{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-31ed4558-6b89-5259-81f7-c1113b514f8f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-34e8d1a7-8446-506e-a289-5e07cc9420e3" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $1$ centered at the origin.

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=x+y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ

\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =((\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2})\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}

$$

$$"] ["question-4a047214-1415-5946-9ec9-da29ccac571a" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$

$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ

$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2} \\  & ={\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Notice that the region $R$  represents one-quarter of the sphere of radius $8$ centered at $(0,-8,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =-16y \\ {\rho }^{2} & =-16\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho +16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

$$

"answer-field-748331ec-5745-5dc8-9854-65c69f6cb19e"] [17592186129266 :knowledge-point/questions "question-ddc59e97-e243-5e27-9d57-5e0f9b714882"] [17592186130455 :tutorial/content "When evaluating triple integrals, it's sometimes easier to change the variables from Cartesian coordinates to spherical polar coordinates.

For example, suppose we want to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R \left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2\right)^{3/2} \: \textrm{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the region enclosed by the sphere of radius $1$ centered at $O,$ as shown below.

![](images/08/0809a74f0aca2b3042b7f8db6783f9d6a13bc84bfc75ddcbb4d3076dbf0a2efd.png)

This integral seems too challenging when written in Cartesian coordinates. However, we should recognize that the problem lends itself to spherical polar coordinates because

- the domain $R$ has a simple spherical polar representation, and

- the integrand $f(x,y,z)=\left(x^2+y^2+z^2\right)^{3/2}$ can also be expressed simply in spherical polar coordinates.

So, let's transform the entire problem to spherical polar coordinates using the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined by

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad

y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 

z = \rho\cos\phi.
$$

The preimage of $R$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the rectangular region $\Delta,$ given by

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (\rho, \theta, \phi) \, : \, 0 \leq \rho \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: 0 \leq \phi \leq \pi \right\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/c2/c2ed8a57c5e66687428a524eb148f96672f3a1ace7fbd28d426de065b2fb5f1f.png)

To express our integral in terms of spherical polar coordinates, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 

\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi.
$$

It can be shown that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant for a spherical change of variables is

$$
\left| \dfrac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2\sin\phi.
$$

Therefore, the change of variables formula is

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 

\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \:  \rho^2\sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi.
$$

Now, let's write our function $f(x,y,z) = \left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2\right)^{3/2}$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & ={({\rho }^{2})}^{3/2} \\  & ={\rho }^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{3}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\rho }^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{\rho }^{5}\,d\rho  \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{6}{\rho }^{6}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =1}\,d\rho  \\  & =-(-1-1)\cdot (2\pi -0)\cdot \frac{1}{6}(1-0) \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186130468 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've used the fact that 

$$
\left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2 \sin{\phi}.
$$

Let's now prove this result.

Given the spherical coordinate transformations

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad

y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 

z = \rho\cos\phi,
$$

we first  calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂x}{∂\theta } & =-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂x}{∂ϕ} & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \frac{∂y}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta } & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂y}{∂ϕ} & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \frac{∂z}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta } & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂ϕ} & =-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-2 \\ -{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=4 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

It is easy to show that the system is inconsistent (i.e., it has no solution). However, in real-world problems, we might want to find an approximate solution to the system. 

Let's formulate the problem a little more rigorously. Firstly, we write down the system in the form $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b\mathbin{:}$
![](images/22/22b8abd4638e579875755f482442cf1dbf89653bd9d396b4a802217e25177839.svg)

We are interested in vectors $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ such that $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is very close to $\mathbf b.$ More precisely, we wish to *minimize the distance* between $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and $\mathbf b.$ Recall that the distance between $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and $\mathbf b$ is given by

$$
\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert.
$$

The smaller the value of $\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert,$ the better our approximation $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ will be. 

In terms of vector subspaces, we wish to find a vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ that lies in $\textrm{Col}(A)$ and is closest to $\mathbf{b}.$
Therefore, $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ must be the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$

![](images/3a/3a1c79036954f0e04212892b7e3d79c75f8cd7b81d7785441f090f89a4eb6faf.png)

It can be shown that ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is found by solving the corresponding **normal equation**, given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

We'll prove this at the end of the lesson. Note that the normal equation is obtained by left-multiplying the equation $A {\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = \mathbf b$ by $A^T.$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix $A^T \! A$ is invertible. Therefore, left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T \! A)^{-1},$ we obtain

$$
{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = (A^T \! A)^{-1}A^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

We now compute the right-hand side as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -4 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,\,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 18\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{99}[\begin{aligned}18 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{33} \\ -\frac{38}{33}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is called the **least-squares solution** of the given system.

**Watch out!** We assumed that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, which guarantees that $A^T \! A\,$ is invertible. However, if the columns of $A$ are linearly *dependent,* then we have to use a different approach to solve the problem."] [17592186129524 :question/problem "The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere $x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 9$ for $x \ge 0$ and $z \ge 0$.

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $1$ centered at $(1,0,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2x$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =2x \\ {\rho }^{2} & =2\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](images/31/31a18ebb9608ff60a4a5ecbcfa8defcb6a64337b126cb5859cb042f1019b1194.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{3z}{\sqrt{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})^{3}}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{3\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}{\sqrt{({\rho }^{2})^{3}}} \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}{{\rho }^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{3z}{\sqrt{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})^{3}}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{3\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}{{\rho }^{2}}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}3\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ[\rho ]_{\rho =0}^{\rho =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ-0)\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & =2\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,d\theta  \\  & =2\cdot [-{sin}^{3}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi /2}\cdot [-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =-\pi /2}^{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =2\cdot [{sin}^{3}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi /2}\cdot [\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =-\pi /2}^{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =2\cdot (1-0)\cdot (1-(-1)) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186130455 :tutorial/content "When evaluating triple integrals, it's sometimes easier to change the variables from Cartesian coordinates to spherical polar coordinates.

For example, suppose we want to evaluate the triple integral

$$\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R \left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2\right)^{3/2} \: \textrm{d}V$$

where $R$ is the region enclosed by the sphere of radius $1$ centered at $O,$ as shown below.

![](images/08/0809a74f0aca2b3042b7f8db6783f9d6a13bc84bfc75ddcbb4d3076dbf0a2efd.png)

This integral seems too challenging when written in Cartesian coordinates. However, we should recognize that the problem lends itself to spherical polar coordinates because

- the domain $R$ has a simple spherical polar representation, and
- the integrand $f(x,y,z)=\left(x^2+y^2+z^2\right)^{3/2}$ can also be expressed simply in spherical polar coordinates.

So, let's transform the entire problem to spherical polar coordinates using the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined by

$$x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad z = \rho\cos\phi.$$

The preimage of $R$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the rectangular region $\Delta,$ given by

$$\Delta = \left\{ (\rho, \theta, \phi) \, : \, 0 \leq \rho \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: 0 \leq \phi \leq \pi \right\},$$

as shown below.

![](images/c2/c2ed8a57c5e66687428a524eb148f96672f3a1ace7fbd28d426de065b2fb5f1f.png)

To express our integral in terms of spherical polar coordinates, we will use the change of variables formula

$$\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi.$$

It can be shown that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant for a spherical change of variables is

$$\left| \dfrac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2\sin\phi.$$

Therefore, the change of variables formula is

$$\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \: \rho^2\sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi.$$

Now, let's write our function $f(x,y,z) = \left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2\right)^{3/2}$ in spherical polar coordinates: $$\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}ϕ) \\ & ={({\rho }^{2})}^{3/2} \\ & ={\rho }^{3}\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain
$$\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{3}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\rho }^{5}\operatorname{sin}ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{\rho }^{5}\,d\rho \\ & =[-\operatorname{cos}ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{6}{\rho }^{6}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =1}\,d\rho \\ & =-(-1-1)\cdot (2\pi -0)\cdot \frac{1}{6}(1-0) \\ & =2\cdot 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{6} \\ & =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}$$"] [17592186130468 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've used the fact that $$\left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2 \sin{\phi}.$$

Let's now prove this result.

Given the spherical coordinate transformations

$$x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad z = \rho\cos\phi,$$

we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ & \,\frac{∂x}{∂\theta } & =-\rho \operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ & \,\frac{∂x}{∂ϕ} & =\rho \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{cos}ϕ \\ \frac{∂y}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ & \,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta } & =\rho \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ & \,\frac{∂y}{∂ϕ} & =\rho \operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}ϕ \\ \frac{∂z}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{cos}ϕ & \,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta } & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂ϕ} & =-\rho \operatorname{sin}ϕ\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ & -\rho \operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{cos}ϕ \\ \operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ & \rho \operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}ϕ \\ \operatorname{cos}ϕ & 0 & -\rho \operatorname{sin}ϕ\end{aligned}| \\ & =\operatorname{cos}ϕ|\begin{aligned}-\rho \operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{cos}ϕ \\ \rho \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ & \rho \operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}ϕ\end{aligned}|-\rho \operatorname{sin}ϕ|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ & -\rho \operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ \\ \operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ\end{aligned}| \\ & =\operatorname{cos}ϕ\cdot (-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}ϕ\operatorname{cos}ϕ({sin}^{2}\theta +{cos}^{2}\theta ))-\rho \operatorname{sin}ϕ\cdot \rho {sin}^{2}ϕ\cdot ({cos}^{2}\theta +{sin}^{2}\theta ) \\ & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}ϕ{cos}^{2}ϕ-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}ϕ{sin}^{2}ϕ \\ & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}ϕ({cos}^{2}ϕ+{sin}^{2}ϕ) \\ & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}ϕ.\end{aligned}$$

Finally, we conclude that $$\left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2 \sin{\phi}.$$"] [17592186130469 :tutorial/content "We can also derive the change of variables formula for spherical polar coordinates using geometry.

Consider a bounded spherical box $R,$ given by

$$R = \big\{ (\rho,\theta,\phi) \: | \: a \leq \rho \leq b, \:\: \alpha \leq \theta \leq \beta, \:\: \gamma \leq \phi \leq \psi \big\}.$$

We can divide each interval into $l,m,$ and $n$ subdivisions such that

$$\Delta\rho = \dfrac{b-a}{l},\qquad \Delta\theta = \dfrac{\beta-\alpha}{m},\qquad \Delta\phi = \dfrac{\psi-\gamma}{n}.$$

This splits the region into "spherical wedges," as shown in the following diagram.

![](images/88/88be4c6a09062321d20ac7f48dfbb6be796cdd6b5bb1b7f6adc49a6ae1da609b.png)

Zooming in on one of these wedges, we obtain a shape resembling a rectangular solid.

![](images/5e/5e5f7acb4d057e856c66e9d5626f81178ca26c0b7ce83cdf7290b1f4c64b1852.png)

Let's note the volume of this solid as $\Delta V.$ To approximate the value of $\Delta V,$ we use the formula for the volume of a rectangular solid:

$$\Delta V \approx lwh$$

Clearly, the height of the rectangular solid is $h = \Delta \rho.$ We can find the remaining dimensions using simple geometry.

First, we need to find the length of the radius $r$ in the $xy$-plane. Using the following triangle and a side-on view of the wedge, we conclude that $r=\rho\sin\phi.$

![](images/01/0122c6c3b813bbe2821dbede794b6027cd69002dd1828925811211045a0d67e8.png)

Let's add this to our diagram.

![](images/d4/d41b538e9bb3add9bae1e3a24c9f87ae282a8b969f0c0dc4acd374ad777de74a.png)

Finally, we can use the arc length formula $s = r \cdot \theta$ to find the length $l$ and width $w.$

![](images/88/882b9243d1189c098aaf6e1e45ca7ec97d480b1f2c3a8fe23d5e39a6c2313ed2.png)

The length of our wedge is $$l = \rho \cdot \Delta\phi = \rho\Delta\phi$$ and the width is $$w = \rho\sin\phi \cdot \Delta\theta = \rho\sin\phi\Delta\theta.$$

Calculating the volume as a rectangular solid, we obtain

$$\begin{aligned}ΔV & \approx lwh \\ & =(\rho Δϕ)\cdot (\rho \operatorname{sin}ϕΔ\theta )\cdot (Δ\rho ) \\ & ={\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}ϕ\,Δϕ\,Δ\theta \,Δ\rho .\end{aligned}$$

As a result, we define the triple integral in spherical coordinates as the limit of a triple Riemann sum, where $(\rho_{ijk},\theta_{ijk},\phi_{ijk})$ being any sample point in the spherical subregion $B{ijk}{:}$

$$\lim\limits_{l,m,n \to \infty} \sum\limits_{i=1}^{l} \sum\limits_{j=1}^{m} \sum\limits_{k=1}^{n} f(\rho_{ijk},\theta_{ijk},\phi_{ijk}) (\rho_{ijk})^2 \sin \phi_{ijk} \:\Delta\rho\:\Delta\theta\:\Delta\phi$$

As we increase the number of subregions, the size of $\Delta\rho,$ $\Delta\theta,$ and $\Delta\phi$ all goes to zero, and the volume of $R$ is more accurately approximated, giving

$$\textrm{d}V = \rho^2 \sin\phi \:\textrm{d}\rho\:\textrm{d}\theta\:\textrm{d}\phi.$$

Therefore, we conclude that if $f(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ is continuous on a spherical box $R = [a,b] \times [\alpha,\beta] \times [\gamma, \psi],$ then $$\iiint\limits_{R} f(\rho,\theta,\phi) \:\textrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{R} f(\rho,\theta,\phi) \rho^2 \sin\phi \:\textrm{d}\rho\:\textrm{d}\theta\:\textrm{d}\phi = \int_{\gamma}^{\psi}\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\int_{a}^{b} f(\rho,\theta,\phi) \rho^2 \sin\phi \:\textrm{d}\rho\:\textrm{d}\theta\:\textrm{d}\phi.$$"]]}

- ${\begin{aligned}0, & (x,y)\in R∖D \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡y+{x}^{2}, & (x,y)\in D\end{aligned}$

$$

$$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given functions.

domain. Now, we'll learn how to define a double integral over a non-rectangular region.

Let's consider the non-rectangular region $D$ enclosed by the circle $x^2+y^2=1$ in the first quadrant, as shown below. 

![](images/e8/e80bcbaff16282f00e7e3df487d78cfbc51bb2e9660dde5e2fc421cd4d70a9af.png)

 

We will define the following double integral over this non-rectangular region:

$$
\iint\limits_{D} (3-x^2-2y^2) \, \textrm{d}A
$$

To do this, we will use the following trick. Let's enclose the region $D$ by a rectangle $R$ with sides parallel to the coordinates axes, as shown below. 

![](images/21/214db95d949a8658e3fdbfea8f54c0e3bf914c11d9ef88e1ca4264d64d360c90.png)

 

Now, we extend our function to $R$ by setting a new function $f(x,y)$ that's equal to $0$ outside $D$ and equals $3-x^2-2y^2$ on $D\mathbin{:}$

![](images/ab/ab8eed93d71415d810f4c8c9b19d690317769e270805a6925d35f5f0e4c9671f.svg)

![](images/43/43288ccc496832a1a78f9fcaaabb4a5841fc79db5d2082dff7d4177005b61d01.png)

 

Although $f(x,y)$ might not be continuous at the boundary of $D,$ the double integral of $f(x,y)$ over the rectangular domain $R$ will exist. 

Therefore, we define our double integral of $3-x^2-2y^2$ over $D$ as 

$$
\iint\limits_D (3-x^2-2y^2) \, \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_R f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A.
$$

Geometrically, the value of the double integral will give us the volume of the solid bounded by the surface $z=3-x^2-2y^2$ over the quarter-circular domain $D.$

**Watch out!** The domain $R$ must not necessarily be the smallest possible rectangle that covers the region $D.$ It can be any rectangular domain that covers $D$ completely." :tutorial/id #uuid Consider the region $D$ shown above. If 

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}x+y, & (x,y)\in R\cap D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,{∬}_{D}(x+y)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

which of the following could be the definition of the rectangular domain $R?$

- $R=[-2,2]\times [-1,1]$
- $R=[0,2]\times [-2,2]$
- $R=[-2,2]\times [-2,2]$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Notice that if $R$ covers $D$ completely and we define 

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}x+y, & (x,y)\in R\cap D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D,\end{aligned}
$$

we obtain

$$
{∬}_{D}(x+y)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given rectangles.

- Rectangles I and II do not cover the region $D.$

- Rectangle III covers the region $D$ completely.

f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}y({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}), & (x,y)\in R\cap D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D,\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186198397 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a898f345-9210-5976-9a42-f415a0e7eaf5" :knowledge-point/title "Performing a Change of Variables in a Triple Integral"}] :question/problem "Consider the finite region $R$ in Cartesian $xyz$-space, given by

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \:1 \leq xy \leq  2, \: 1 \leq y \leq 2, \: 0 \leq z\leq 1 \big\}.
$$

By performing the change of variables

$$
u=xy,  \qquad
v=y, \qquad
w=2z,
$$

 

write down the triple integral

$$
\displaystyle 
\iiint\limits_R 3xy^2+6yz \, \mathrm{d}V
$$

as a repeated integral in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

![](images/c3/c3c03fec53fda9106ca287f15afd0d07b1adddf00675b2bdbec8a658fbdf06aa.png)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \ \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v,w), y(u,v,w), z(u,v,w)) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \right|  \: \textrm{d}u \textrm{d}v \textrm{d}w
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=xy,  \qquad
v=y, \qquad
w=2z,
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](images/64/643fb7a9bbc46ac2a6fe8c6d89f4fcb7f2db206c7af11f7cde9e1a34da8ac201.png)

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(u,v,w)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 2,\,0\le w\le 2}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}y & x & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2|\begin{aligned}y & x \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(y-0) \\  & =2y \\  & =2v.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} \right)^{-1} =\dfrac{1}{2v}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf{T}$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}3x{y}^{2}+6yz\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}(3uv+3vw)\cdot |\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}3v(u+w)\cdot |\frac{1}{2v}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3}{2}(u+w)\,dw\,dv\,du\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048839} {:db/id 17592186049530} {:db/id 17592186050482} {:db/id 17592186198959 :question/id #uuid "96fa59d6-c144-5393-a4a7-7b8198eb987c" :question/math-academy-id "q-38941"} {:db/id 17592186198963 :question/id #uuid "9d27a7ac-3737-5071-b997-af83c998bd7d" :question/math-academy-id "q-39054" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198397 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a898f345-9210-5976-9a42-f415a0e7eaf5" :knowledge-point/title "Performing a Change of Variables in a Triple Integral"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "efccd2f5-3dcb-549b-a791-9a953c0859ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sin u\cos v" :db/id 17592186197649} {:answer/id #uuid "01110ca9-4f16-5a77-ade5-867fbcd28671" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2\sin u\cos v" :db/id 17592186197650} {:answer/id #uuid "28f56d8e-e1c7-5447-a918-701e450eabeb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\sin u\cos v" :db/id 17592186197651} {:answer/id #uuid "46f32d0b-96ea-5d4d-8468-c29158bdc3a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3\sin u\cos v" :db/id 17592186197652} {:answer/id #uuid "721547b0-a678-5c59-b301-7880bb72ccba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}\sin u\cos v" :db/id 17592186197653}] :answer-field/id #uuid "92bb2c37-88bf-542c-b72c-3da1ea32bcd2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186197648}] :question/problem "Consider the finite region $R$ in the $xyz$-space, given by

:knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Triple Integral Using a Change of Variables"}] :question/problem "Use the change of variables 

$$
u = x+y^2, \qquad
v=  y+z, \qquad
w = 2z
$$

to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\displaystyle 
\iiint \limits_R (x+y^2)^{15}z \: \mathrm{d}V,
$$

 
where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \:  0 \leq x+y^2 \leq 1, \: 0 \leq y+z \leq 4, \: 0\leq z\leq 2 \big\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

![](images/eb/eb8f40c6ffabf36ae5a305c7c7b71683b914b537f64766a20aac09d3666fac81.png)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \ \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v,w), y(u,v,w), z(u,v,w)) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \right|  \: \textrm{d}u \textrm{d}v \textrm{d}w
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u = x+y^2, \qquad
v=  y+z, \qquad
w = 2z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](images/4b/4bcd5430181c2cb411dfe984b04399f2f80ab9d1747d5cf82596d105419b2b4f.png)

To compute the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(u,v,w)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 4,\,0\le w\le 4}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2y & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot 1\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} \right)^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf{T}$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}(x+{y}^{2})^{15}z\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}{u}^{15}\cdot \frac{w}{2}\cdot |\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{∭}_{Δ}{u}^{15}w\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{4}{u}^{15}w\,dw\,dv\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{15}\,du\cdot {\int }_{0}^{4}dv\cdot {\int }_{0}^{4}w\,dw \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot [\frac{{u}^{16}}{16}]_{u=0}^{u=1}\cdot {[v]}_{v=0}^{v=4}\cdot [\frac{{w}^{2}}{2}]_{w=0}^{w=4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot (\frac{1}{16}-0)\cdot (4-0)\cdot (8-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198623 :question/id #uuid "1d5d9726-730c-531d-b668-66f3dda1040e" :question/math-academy-id "q-162139" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198398 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "832dc2b8-873f-56c6-bd87-5e886a586fb1" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Triple Integral Using a Change of Variables"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8f646c61-db32-5905-849a-04ada136657a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186194370} {:answer/id #uuid "dda01489-76a5-59ec-9704-87adeb52fd5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186194371} {:answer/id #uuid "18c290d7-6b8d-50ae-99c2-f0eb7045b012" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186194372} {:answer/id #uuid "1935b921-c755-5f9b-b2fd-fdf3102bd3a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186194373} {:answer/id #uuid "494337ce-d303-53d0-97cd-b0e1b611d95e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186194374}] :answer-field/id #uuid "cb5cc458-53cc-5d59-888b-d4167a5b9c4d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186194369}] :question/problem "Use the change of variables

"e-12408" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186198399 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a8a79d4e-f9e0-583e-8e52-aa60c14fd4a3" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Volume of a Region Using a Change of Variables"}] :question/problem "Find the volume bounded by the region $R,$ given by

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x+y \leq 1, \:-2 \leq y-2x \leq 2, \: 1 \leq z^3 \leq 8 \big\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the volume of $R$ can be found as 

$$
V = \iiint\limits_R \textrm{d}V.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

![](images/54/54035a0d0a2dd88eb0b4b89bb1162df2cf9b450a4ea4d5b5020163053880016f.png)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required volume, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \ \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v,w), y(u,v,w), z(u,v,w)) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \right|  \: \textrm{d}u \textrm{d}v \textrm{d}w
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

The inequalities that define the region $R,$

$$
0 \leq x+y \leq 1, \qquad
-2 \leq y-2x \leq 2, \qquad
1 \leq z^3 \leq 8,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u = x+y, \qquad
v = y-2x, \qquad
w = z^3.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](images/4b/4bcd5430181c2cb411dfe984b04399f2f80ab9d1747d5cf82596d105419b2b4f.png)

To compute the required volume, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(u,v,w)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,-2\le v\le 2,\,1\le w\le 8}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3{z}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =3{z}^{2}(-1)^{3+3}|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =9{z}^{2} \\  & =9{w}^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} \right)^{-1} = \dfrac 19 w^{-2/3}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf{T}$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}dV & ={∭}_{Δ}1\cdot |\frac{1}{9}{w}^{-2/3}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{8}\frac{1}{9}{w}^{-2/3}\,dw\,dv\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{\int }_{0}^{1}du\cdot {\int }_{-2}^{2}dv\cdot {\int }_{1}^{8}{w}^{-2/3}dw \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[u]_{0}^{1}\cdot [v]_{-2}^{2}\cdot [3{w}^{1/3}]_{1}^{8} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot (1-0)\cdot (2-(-2))\cdot 3({8}^{1/3}-{1}^{1/3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048997} {:db/id 17592186198624 :question/id #uuid "51e25390-3ec9-57e6-8340-3c34fe595d12" :question/math-academy-id "q-162149"} {:db/id 17592186198965 :question/id #uuid "8b45928b-ff82-5faf-a3d8-f16998390abd" :question/math-academy-id "q-39060" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198399 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a8a79d4e-f9e0-583e-8e52-aa60c14fd4a3" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Volume of a Region Using a Change of Variables"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "881b0dd0-01c6-5013-9685-0e58c6da71c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186197661} {:answer/id #uuid "c8a11a8a-6503-5229-93d1-630340faec00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186197662} {:answer/id #uuid "33e5fb8a-a7fa-5959-b381-9183f9303802" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}" :db/id 17592186197663} {:answer/id #uuid "3404d280-8cad-5644-8ec1-3e6e08824288" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186197664} {:answer/id #uuid "4cd7243b-48c8-50fa-aaa2-6aa1ef439e80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186197665}] :answer-field/id #uuid "3cd3b3e1-98ae-532b-94b3-c5b9b8ab641b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186197660}] :question/problem "Find the volume bounded by the region $R$, given by

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186199269 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199461 :tutorial/content "Suppose that the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by

$$\mathbf T: (u,v,w) \longrightarrow \left(x(u,v,w), \, y(u,v,w), \, z(u,v,w) \right)$$

is a $C^1$ transformation that has no critical points (i.e., it is invertible) inside some region $\Delta\subset \mathbb R^3,$ and that $\mathbf T(\Delta) = R,$ as shown below.

![](images/d7/d7875753545cba8babd08fccaf55236c6b32bfc56f43f496343174acc198f1d9.png)

To compute the integral of a function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R,$ we use the change of variables formula

$$\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \ \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v,w), y(u,v,w), z(u,v,w)) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \right| \: \textrm{d}u \textrm{d}v \textrm{d}w$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

Note the similarity with the change of variables formula for double integrals." :tutorial/id #uuid "a43397ab-8a32-5928-ba64-90ad84532ab1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7217 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} given by

${0,\begin{vmatrix}x < 1, \\ 1 - \frac{1}{x^{4}},\end{vmatrix}x \ge 1$." :question/worked-solution "The median of a random variable $X$ is the number $m$ such that

$$
P(X \leq m) = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
P(X \leq m) = F(m) = 1-\dfrac{1}{m^4}, \quad m \geq 1
$$

Therefore, the median is given by

$$
1-\dfrac{1}{m^4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\quad \Rightarrow \quad m = \sqrt[4]2
$$

Note that we took the positive root because

$$
m \geq 1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049697} {:db/id 17592186050750} {:db/id 17592186162626 :question/id #uuid "351e4dd6-4e2c-5502-8929-c967c832d159" :question/math-academy-id "q-94432"} {:db/id 17592186162640 :question/id #uuid "6953abf3-1fc1-5585-929d-c6274d97e098" :question/math-academy-id "q-94564"} {:db/id 17592186161998 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161790 :question/id #uuid "d22e7154-ac3c-5ac6-ad86-77a7eb08f82e" :question/math-academy-id "e-8238"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a79c4207-c5d6-5386-818e-a7e532492732" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049638}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162332 :question/id #uuid "79ec3e35-8825-5148-9c85-135ddfc568c9" :question/math-academy-id "q-125775"} {:db/id 17592186162627 :question/id #uuid "11b61c93-9964-5c89-b85a-5bd388eb8259" :question/math-academy-id "q-94433"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Median Given the PDF a Continuous Random Variable"} {:db/id 17592186161790 :question/id #uuid "d22e7154-ac3c-5ac6-ad86-77a7eb08f82e" :question/math-academy-id "e-8238" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186161998 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a79c4207-c5d6-5386-818e-a7e532492732" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Median Given the PDF a Continuous Random Variable"}] :question/problem "Find the median of the random variable $X$ if the probability density function of $X$ is given by

${0,\begin{vmatrix}x < 1, \\ \frac{2}{x^{3}},\end{vmatrix}x \ge 1$." :question/worked-solution "The median of a random variable $X$ is the number $m$ such that

$$
P(X \leq m) = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X \le m) &= \int_{1}^{m}\frac{2}{x^{3}}dx \\
&= \left.- \frac{1}{x^{2}}\right|_{1}^{m} \\
&=-\frac{1}{m^{2}} + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the median is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
-\frac{1}{m^{2}} + 1 &= \frac{1}{2} \\
\frac{1}{m^{2}} &= \frac{1}{2} \\
m &= \sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we took the positive root because

$$
m \geq 1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049638} {:db/id 17592186162332 :question/id #uuid "79ec3e35-8825-5148-9c85-135ddfc568c9" :question/math-academy-id "q-125775"} {:db/id 17592186162627 :question/id #uuid "11b61c93-9964-5c89-b85a-5bd388eb8259" :question/math-academy-id "q-94433"} {:db/id 17592186161999 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161791 :question/id #uuid "3be25e37-7162-5565-86d2-47ea69c599ce" :question/math-academy-id "e-8239"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "563f7ff5-8ebb-5130-badb-f092fa348959" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050081}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162628 :question/id #uuid "ebd7a71e-1f73-5bd8-af6b-f7f521da9dae" :question/math-academy-id "q-94434"} {:db/id 17592186162641 :question/id #uuid "1e1b7e9e-2574-5316-a0b8-5178c531c66d" :question/math-academy-id "q-94576"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Quartile of a Continuous Random Variable"} {:db/id 17592186161791 :question/id #uuid "3be25e37-7162-5565-86d2-47ea69c599ce" :question/math-academy-id "e-8239" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186161999 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "563f7ff5-8ebb-5130-badb-f092fa348959" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Quartile of a Continuous Random Variable"}] :question/problem "Find, to three decimal places, the interquartile range of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

${0,\begin{vmatrix}x < 0, \\ \frac{x^{2}}{25},\end{vmatrix}0 \le x \le 5,; 1, \mid x > 5$." :question/worked-solution "To find the interquartile range, we first need to find the lower quartile and the upper quartile.

The lower quartile of a random variable $X$ is the number $q_1$ such that

$$
P(X \leq q_1) = \dfrac{1}{4}
$$

and the upper quartile is the number $q_3$ such that

$$
P(X \leq q_3) = \dfrac{3}{4}
$$

First, we find the lower quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X \le q_{1}) &= \frac{1}{4} \\
F(q_{1}) &= \frac{1}{4} \\
\frac{1}{25}q_{1}^{2} &= \frac{1}{4} \\
q_{1}^{2} &= \frac{25}{4} \\
q_{1} &= \frac{5}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the upper quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X \le q_{3}) &= \frac{3}{4} \\
F(q_{3}) &= \frac{3}{4} \\
\frac{1}{25}q_{3}^{2} &= \frac{3}{4} \\
q_{3}^{2} &= \frac{75}{4} \\
q_{3} &= \frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the interquartile range is

$$
IQR = q_3 - q_1 =\dfrac{5\sqrt3}{2} - \dfrac{5}{2}\approx 1.830
$$

rounded to three decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186050081} {:db/id 17592186162628 :question/id #uuid "ebd7a71e-1f73-5bd8-af6b-f7f521da9dae" :question/math-academy-id "q-94434"} {:db/id 17592186162641 :question/id #uuid "1e1b7e9e-2574-5316-a0b8-5178c531c66d" :question/math-academy-id "q-94576" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186161999 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "563f7ff5-8ebb-5130-badb-f092fa348959" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Quartile of a Continuous Random Variable"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8eb81564-9ad5-59dc-9e15-1e7c5d7a547e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\ln (4) - \ln (3)" :db/id 17592186161139} {:answer/id #uuid "abb16d90-b8bc-5b89-a8c2-8910ef74798a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\ln (4)" :db/id 17592186161140} {:answer/id #uuid "ddecf1d0-05b6-54d2-9db3-626fcba9cf4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\ln (3) - \ln (4)" :db/id 17592186161141} {:answer/id #uuid "0c5a28d5-56db-5e59-a8d4-992720b4b22b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\ln (3)" :db/id 17592186161142} {:answer/id #uuid "467021a3-fd5c-52cf-a6a4-8b16a64194b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\ln (2)" :db/id 17592186161143}] :answer-field/id #uuid "43bc050a-7f4d-5ec6-bef2-a525c0cde7b4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186161138}] :question/problem "Find the interquartile range of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

${\frac{2}{75}x,\begin{vmatrix}5 \le x \le 10, \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise$." :question/worked-solution "The $100p$th percentile of a random variable $X$ is the number $x_p$ such that

$$
P(X \leq x_p) = p
$$

In our case, we want to find the $27$th percentile, which corresponds to the decimal $p=0.27$. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X \le x_{0.27}) &= \int_{5}^{x_{0.27}}\frac{2}{75}xdx \\
&= \left.\frac{x^{2}}{75}\right|_{5}^{x_{0.27}} \\
&= \frac{x_{0.27}^{2}}{75} - \frac{1}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $27$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{x_{0.27}^{2}}{75} - \frac{1}{3} &= 0.27 \\
x_{0.27}^{2} &= 75(\frac{27}{100} + \frac{1}{3}) \\
x_{0.27} &= 6.727
\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186162629 :question/id #uuid "a82afd35-8f64-55e9-bf5d-d20f47ccbc94" :question/math-academy-id "q-94435"} {:db/id 17592186162644 :question/id #uuid "7bfa7b9d-151d-5ab9-bbf5-f49790dd348d" :question/math-academy-id "q-94701" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162000 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "84b181c4-fc23-5a68-8042-55f02b1e5e8a" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Percentile of a Continuous Random Variable"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "aa2483e3-c0fb-5c8d-af32-3a22222495f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\ln (7) - \ln (10)" :db/id 17592186161157} {:answer/id #uuid "dfa62c87-a339-5b83-a7de-fd14f913a580" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\ln (10) - \ln (3)" :db/id 17592186161158} {:answer/id #uuid "2a9d8daf-5754-56c2-8d76-dd374933430e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\ln (3) - \ln (10)" :db/id 17592186161159} {:answer/id #uuid "41a075a4-7f21-56bf-b533-aae8adec6477" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\ln (10) - \ln (7)" :db/id 17592186161160} {:answer/id #uuid "68bb5f18-1690-5a19-be8b-5fe88c87fc18" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\ln (7) - \ln (3)" :db/id 17592186161161}] :answer-field/id #uuid "7ef4dfd0-f0cc-51fe-86d6-3a8aa37b7302" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186161156}] :question/problem "Find the $30$th percentile of the random variable $Y$ if the probability distribution function of $Y$ is given by

\ln (3)" :db/id 17592186161161} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186162882} :activity/id #uuid "4407446b-5fc6-5ec1-a901-75a95c2caa7b" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048871 :topic/id #uuid "c80985c0-d51a-5f21-9b71-21587d8d82cc" :topic/math-academy-id 3024} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186162882 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163239 :tutorial/content "If $X$ is a continuous random variable and

$$
0 \leq p \leq 1
$$

then the $100p$th **percentile** is a number $x_p$ such that

$$
P(X \leq x_p) = p
$$

- In terms of CDF, the *cumulative distribution function* $F(x)$ of $X$, the $100p$th percentile $x_p$ is a number on the $x$-axis such that

$$
F(x_p) = p
$$

- In terms of PDF, the *probability density function* $f(x)$ of $X$, the $100p$th percentile $x_p$ is a number on the $x$-axis such that the area under the graph of $y=f(x)$ to the left of $x$ is equal to $p$:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{x_p} f(x) \, \text{d}x = p
$$

For example, let's find the $4$th percentile of the random variable $X$ if the probability density function of $X$ is given by

$$
{\frac{1}{2}x,\begin{vmatrix}0 \le x \le 2, \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$

The $4$th percentile corresponds to the decimal

$$
p={\color{red}0.04}
$$

since

$$
100 \cdot 0.04 = 4
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X \le x_{0.04}) &= \int_{0}^{x_{0.04}}\frac{1}{2}xdx \\
&= \left.\frac{x^{2}}{4}\right|_{0}^{x_{0.04}} \\
&= \frac{x_{0.04}^{2}}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $4$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{x_{0.04}^{2}}{4} &= 0.04 \\
x_{0.04}^{2} &= 0.16 \\
x_{0.04} &= 0.4
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we took the positive root because

$$
0 \leq x_{0.04} \leq 2
$$

There are a few special percentiles:

- the $25$th percentile is called the **lower quartile**. This is the number $q_1$ such that
$P(X \leq q_1) = 0.25$.
- the $50$th percentile is called the **median**. This is the number $m$ such that
$P(X \leq m) = 0.5$.
- the $75$th percentile is called the **upper quartile**. This is the number $q_3$ such that
$P(X \leq q_3) = 0.75$.
- the **interquartile range** is the difference between the upper and lower quartiles, that is,
$IQR = q_3 - q_1$." :tutorial/id #uuid "e91993d1-ae51-5742-8eeb-e76348c0b8af" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4942 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b587e6fa-53fb-5f03-9ffa-373892fc4d10" $$
(a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2
$$

Substituting $a=2n^2$ and $b=3$, we have

$$"} {:db/id 17592186064592 :question/id #uuid "c237a887-3f0a-5930-a091-6bbeb65a51dd" :question/math-academy-id "q-216486"} {:db/id 17592186064593 :question/id #uuid "9b86fc74-e343-566e-b44e-ca6552a831c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-216503"} {:db/id 17592186064729 :question/id #uuid "4b2fa448-ba75-59e1-a5cd-f450f770f18b" :question/math-academy-id "q-31197"} {:db/id 17592186064234 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063993 :question/id #uuid "487f1c4c-63c9-51cf-9a0e-7d9bc0a4c7c7" :question/math-academy-id "e-14320"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "afd30bc7-dce9-5e03-a213-2b9695e39091" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064591 :question/id #uuid "26571045-d246-5d1d-b740-bb2f14694ebb" :question/math-academy-id "q-215916"} {:db/id 17592186064594 :question/id #uuid "27faa07c-100b-5aa1-a0e3-2028f11459de" :question/math-academy-id "q-216525"} {:db/id 17592186064679 :question/id #uuid "37fc65b4-fc5d-5478-88a6-a76de5f7b167" :question/math-academy-id "q-2678"}] :knowledge-point/title "Squaring Binomials With Subtraction"} {:db/id 17592186063993 :question/id #uuid "487f1c4c-63c9-51cf-9a0e-7d9bc0a4c7c7" :question/math-academy-id "e-14320" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186064234 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "afd30bc7-dce9-5e03-a213-2b9695e39091" :knowledge-point/title "Squaring Binomials With Subtraction"}] :question/problem "Expand $(3p - 5)^2$." :question/worked-solution "We will use the following formula:

**square of a binomial**, like

$$
(a+b)^2
$$

there's a formula that we can use instead of working out the product $(a+b)(a+b)$ manually. The formula is

$$
(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2
$$

It might be helpful to remember this as *"the square of the first term, plus the square of the second term, plus twice the product."*

Suppose we need to calculate the square $(x+3)^2$. In this case, we have $a= x$ and $b=3$. We substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(x + 3)^{2} &=  \\
(x)^{2} + 2(x)(3) + (3)^{2} &=  \\
&= x^{2} + 6x + 9
\end{aligned}
$$

We can check that the formula gives the correct result by working out the multiplication manually:

$$
\begin{aligned} (x + 3)^2 \\[3pt] &= (x + 3)(x + 3) \\[3pt] &= x(x + 3) + 3(x + 3) \\[3pt] &= x^2 + 3x + 3x + 9 \\[3pt] &= x^2 + 6x + 9 &\, {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{aligned}
$$

So we get the same result! But by using the formula, we save a lot of time and effort." :tutorial/id #uuid "0266d886-b5db-53fe-bc51-f6486beb6eef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8878 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ee3a0134-3957-5b1c-b05a-a30af1c8709d" :step/math-academy-id 170779 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065098}} {:db/id 17592186065098 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064232 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063991 :question/id #uuid "70f19ea4-d0b8-537a-8ae4-06a236cf37cf" :question/math-academy-id "e-14318"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "288c08af-0583-5588-b767-4254544cf70c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050818}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064590} {:db/id 17592186064678} {:db/id 17592186064749}] :knowledge-point/title "Squaring Linear Binomials"} :step/id #uuid "39924b31-d2c9-5359-be1b-3c04f7ad4699" :step/math-academy-id 170780 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065099}} {:db/id 17592186065099 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064233 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063992 :question/id #uuid "c1a6df9e-b1e8-51c8-b5df-4cc624e14193" :question/math-academy-id "e-14319"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "63291c46-6a0f-5e7c-ab0a-acba80fe58f3" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064592} {:db/id 17592186064593} {:db/id 17592186064729}] :knowledge-point/title "Squaring Nonlinear Binomials"} :step/id #uuid "9b092f72-50ae-5b82-96c3-f01cc623e041" :step/math-academy-id 170784 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065100}} {:db/id 17592186065100 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065442 :tutorial/content "So far, we've been using the formula for the square of a binomial involving addition:

$$

There is also a similar formula that we can use to compute the square of a binomial involving subtraction. The formula is

$$
(a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2
$$

For example, to compute the square $(x-3)^2$, we can substitute $a=x$ and $b=3$ into the formula and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(x - 3)^{2} &=  \\
(x)^{2} - 2(x)(3) + (3)^{2} &=  \\
&= x^{2} - 6x + 9
\end{aligned}
$$

We can check that the formula gives the correct result by working out the multiplication manually:

$$
\begin{aligned} (x - 3)^2 \\ &= (x - 3)(x - 3) \\ &= x(x - 3) - 3(x - 3) \\ &= x^2 - 3x - 3x + 9 \\ &= x^2 - 6x + 9 &\, {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{aligned}
$$

:tutorial/content "Let's take a look at the following algebraic expression:

$$
2x{\,\color{red}{-}\,} 4y {\,\color{blue}{+}\,} 7
$$

The addition $({\color{blue}{+}})$ and subtraction $({\color{red}{-}})$ symbols separate this expression into three parts known as **terms**.  

To identify each term, we put an addition symbol $({\color{blue}{+}})$ between each part and separate using parentheses:

$$
(2x) {\,\color{blue}{+}\,} ({\,\color{red}{-}\,} 4y) {\,\color{blue}{+}\,} (7).
$$

So, the terms of this expression are: 

$$
2x,\quad -4y,\quad  \quad 7
$$

We say that $2x$ is the **first term**, $-4y$ is the **second term**, and $7$ is the **third term**. 

In this example, the subtraction symbol gave us the term $-4y$. Whenever there is a subtraction symbol, the corresponding term will be negative." :tutorial/id #uuid "a3fedc83-1abf-5dae-af95-68dd8069bf3e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8035 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f8931686-8ab0-55f7-ac91-27963af09ae5" :step/math-academy-id 75175 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079590}} {:db/id 17592186079590 :step/content {:db/id 17592186078613 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078158 :question/id #uuid "65cb74a2-b55a-58e7-951d-2e0c09662f68" :question/math-academy-id "e-12823"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ffb52c1b-a540-5255-8c13-a37940a0d6ec" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050618} {:db/id 17592186051009}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078812} {:db/id 17592186079038} {:db/id 17592186079039} {:db/id 17592186444245} {:db/id 17592186444248} {:db/id 17592186444251} {:db/id 17592186444254} {:db/id 17592186444255}] :knowledge-point/title "Listing the Terms of a Linear Expression"} :step/id #uuid "d3ccacbe-b3b1-59d6-aca9-544e52d96477" :step/math-academy-id 75176 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079591}} {:db/id 17592186079591 :step/content {:db/id 17592186078614 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078159 :question/id #uuid "4370fda3-97e7-5fc5-9459-4176f5922431" :question/math-academy-id "e-12824"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "da99f266-f47f-5fda-8b91-2161c7e48a94" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078900} {:db/id 17592186078901} {:db/id 17592186079175} {:db/id 17592186444246} {:db/id 17592186444249} {:db/id 17592186444250} {:db/id 17592186444252}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Particular Terms of an Expression"} :step/id #uuid "a41ca648-ff16-5981-9555-fc4f21dbf835" :step/math-academy-id 75180 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079592}} {:db/id 17592186079592 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079715 :tutorial/content "When two algebraic expressions contain exactly the same terms, they are said to be **equivalent**.

$$

$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In our case, we have

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane  $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 5 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}9 & -5 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that we obtained ${\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=x.$ This simply means that $x$ lies in the plane, i.e., 

$$
x\in \text{Span}{v,w}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186382518 :question/id #uuid "e3585dd8-8fa2-556f-ac24-bf117ff60918" :question/math-academy-id "q-83588"} {:db/id 17592186388716 :question/id #uuid
