{:db/id 17592186049970 :topic/id #uuid "22979210-8cd9-5db4-861d-faf167d0a850" :topic/math-academy-id 2124} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134674 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135049 :tutorial/content "We've already seen how to find the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace in the case when the subspace is defined using an orthogonal basis. In this lesson, we'll learn how to do the same thing in the case of non-orthogonal bases.

For example, consider the following vectors:
![](images/28/28ce7470231775d8889555d0dd9f37ee9215044762a40335bd43578b121486a3.svg)
How can we find the orthogonal projection $\mathbf{x}_S$ of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}?$ Notice that since $\mathbf a_1\cdot \mathbf a_2 \neq 0,$ the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are not orthogonal.

As usual, we would like to write $\mathbf{x}$ as 

$$
\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_S + \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp},
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \in S$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \!\in S^\perp.$

![](images/3a/3a5576fcaf9e0be6fc14978eb91dcbaceee75cbfddaa537fdb05d34b8e31e2e0.png)

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\  & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\  & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp,$ that is, $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \perp S,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{1} \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{2}\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the expression for $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ into the system to get
![](images/f1/f1e3c7ae9e966ebcab88901c9e44a5449cb98716f43fc526d306e0af5186923b.svg)

We can write this system in an equivalent matrix form as follows:
![](images/47/472c41e1e509d2db9c41dfa95127382eeba7ab5fbaa4172d680c39335694ef2e.svg)

If we denote 
![](images/26/2650c1020d413a7c988279cc698ab4b7c4caff427615d49b35ef4e9a42651ff0.svg)
and ![](images/9b/9b50884bd0af404e71f9d7734e9bc054fc9439aba02780cf2beb5fa0a6ac1f32.svg) then we obtain

$$
A^TA\mathbf{k} = A^T\mathbf{x}
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	\mathbf{k}=(A^TA)^{-1}A^T\mathbf{x}.
$$

Also, we note that  $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2$ can be expressed as $\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x}	= A\mathbf{k}.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =Ak \\  & =A({A}^{T}A)^{-1}{A}^{T}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a formula for the orthogonal projection!

Now, we return to our example. Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ 8 & 11\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}11 & -8 \\ -8 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Note**: Pay attention to the order in which we carried out the multiplication. Carrying out the operations in the order shown above can save us a lot of work!" :tutorial/id #uuid "0a9a954f-9338-5c3f-a9db-9b39a1a60c0b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3626 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f3cce71c-fd0d-5040-949b-813f3fdcbdd7" :step/math-academy-id 20246 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134676}} {:db/id 17592186134675 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133788 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133597 :question/id #uuid "b8bbe0e1-8bf1-5b3a-a77e-6350ea77e83f" :question/math-academy-id "e-5575"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ad9f55b2-ce37-507f-8cb6-7d4e30e6868a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134296} {:db/id 17592186134301} {:db/id 17592186272103} {:db/id 17592186275452} {:db/id 17592186326787} {:db/id 17592186326854} {:db/id 17592186366111} {:db/id 17592186382580} {:db/id 17592186388723} {:db/id 17592186388960} {:db/id 17592186388967} {:db/id 17592186388974} {:db/id 17592186392354}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace"} :step/id #uuid "8e0f305d-efdf-586e-b799-66fe2b5a8f6a" :step/math-academy-id 20247 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134678}} {:db/id 17592186134676 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135050 :tutorial/content "If $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is a set of *linearly independent* vectors, then the orthogonal projection of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x},
$$

 
where $A$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n,$ that is,
![](images/25/25a85721a3721ace1a32f6ed457749091452df93053d2eba7dbfaa48f6f74189.svg)

**Watch out!** The fact that $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ must be linearly independent is important. If the vectors are linearly dependent, we need to find the basis of the span before applying the formula." :tutorial/id #uuid "3274de58-5861-55c3-9614-08540ad4231e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3627 :tutorial/title "The General Formula for the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace"} :step/id #uuid "c20a2e38-a98a-579e-9564-09d78a7f10c9" :step/math-academy-id 20248 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134677}} {:db/id 17592186134677 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133789 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133598 :question/id #uuid "ac8363a8-fc77-52e0-b060-5e3a45c5171a" :question/math-academy-id "e-5576"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c07721dd-4b97-5d57-8de1-5098117e3071" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049548} {:db/id 17592186050009} {:db/id 17592186050308} {:db/id 17592186050727}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134240} {:db/id 17592186134243} {:db/id 17592186275463} {:db/id 17592186326855} {:db/id 17592186351518} {:db/id 17592186354508} {:db/id 17592186365003} {:db/id 17592186365171} {:db/id 17592186381153} {:db/id 17592186382518} {:db/id 17592186388716} {:db/id 17592186389002} {:db/id 17592186394511} {:db/id 17592186394518} {:db/id 17592186394738}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane"} :step/id #uuid "184ad4b9-e662-5d0f-9c92-14f6b77fcc1f" :step/math-academy-id 20249 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134675}} {:db/id 17592186134678 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135051 :tutorial/content "As we've already seen, the orthogonal projection of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the one-dimensional subspace $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ is given by 

$$
\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}} \, \mathbf{x} = \dfrac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}} \: \mathbf{a}.
$$

If we suppose that $\mathbf{a}$ denotes the column-vector ![](images/c2/c23a26d5ce1137e222e28a4bc872f9bcffda2cd6430f2d5532618ccf0ed95fa5.svg) then the dot product $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}$ is simply $\mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{a},$ and we can write the formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{(a\cdot x)}{(a\cdot a)}\,a \\  & =[\frac{({a}^{T}x)}{({a}^{T}a)}]a \\  & =a[\frac{({a}^{T}x)}{({a}^{T}a)}] \\  & =a[({a}^{T}a)^{-1}{a}^{T}x] \\  & =a\,({a}^{T}a)^{-1}{a}^{T}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's compare the above with the formula that we use when we want to project onto an arbitrary subspace:

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}
$$

 
As we can see, they are basically the same thing!" :tutorial/id #uuid "491ffb4a-98e5-59b5-8c01-3d23f872cc3f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3628 :tutorial/title "Some Intuition Behind the Formula"} :step/id #uuid "5b14c806-2358-52c9-aabe-db4086c3d1ef" :step/math-academy-id 20250}] :activity/title "Projecting Vectors Onto Subspaces in Euclidean Spaces (Arbitrary Bases)" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134003} {:db/id 17592186134674 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135049 :tutorial/content "We've already seen how to find the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace in the case when the subspace is defined using an orthogonal basis. \begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ 8 & 11\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}11 & -8 \\ -8 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Carrying out the operations in the order shown above can save us a lot of work!" :tutorial/id #uuid "0a9a954f-9338-5c3f-a9db-9b39a1a60c0b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3626 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186134676 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135050 :tutorial/content "If $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is a set of *linearly independent* vectors, then the orthogonal projection of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x},
$$

 
where $A$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n,$ that is,
![](images/25/25a85721a3721ace1a32f6ed457749091452df93053d2eba7dbfaa48f6f74189.svg)

$$
\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}} \, \mathbf{x} = \dfrac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}} \: \mathbf{a}.
$$

If we suppose that $\mathbf{a}$ denotes the column-vector ![](images/c2/c23a26d5ce1137e222e28a4bc872f9bcffda2cd6430f2d5532618ccf0ed95fa5.svg) then the dot product $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}$ is simply $\mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{a},$ and we can write the formula as follows:

$$

$$

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}
$$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y=8xy+2-8e.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,e).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =8xy+2-8e \\ 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy & =2-8e\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=2-8e.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,e)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,e)={f}_{y}(1,e)\,i-{f}_{x}(1,e)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{2x}{y}-8x)i-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8y)\,j \\ t(1,e) & =(\frac{2(1)}{e}-8(1))i-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡e-8(e))\,j \\  & =(\frac{2}{e}-8)i+(8e-2)j\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, our tangent vector is $(\frac{2}{e}-8)i+(8e-2)\,j.$"} {:db/id 17592186339107 :question/id #uuid "148b9435-dbdc-5e2a-8580-1b7906c6cec6" :question/math-academy-id "q-72400"} {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "At which points on the curve ${y}^{2}+2xy={x}^{2}+8$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $j?$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.

- **I.** $(-2,-2)$
- **II.** $(0,2)$
- **III.** $(1,2)$
- **IV.** $(2,0)$
- **V.** $(2,1)$
- **VI.** $(2,2)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2xy & ={x}^{2}+8 \\ {y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2} & =8\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=8.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2})j \\  & =2(y+x)\,i-2(y-x)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $j$, we must have $t\cdot j=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ (2(y+x)\,i-2(y-x)\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -2(y-x) & =0 \\ y & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ (x)^{2}+2x(x)-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ {x}^{2}+2{x}^{2}-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =8 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=2$, we get $y=2$ and the corresponding point is $(2,2).$

- If $x=-2$, we get $y=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-2,-2).$"} {:db/id 17592186339115 :question/id #uuid "5577e429-0d55-5dd4-b588-49ac727edd6b" :question/math-academy-id "q-72440"} {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "At which points on the curve $2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=-y$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $j?$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.

- **I.** $(-1,1)$
- **II.** $(0,0)$
- **III.** $(0,\frac{1}{3})$
- **IV.** $(1,1)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+y)\,j \\  & =(-6y+1)\,i-4x\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $j,$ we must have $t\cdot j=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ ((-6y+1)\,i-4x\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -4x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=0$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 2({0}^{2})-3{y}^{2} & =-y \\ 3{y}^{2}-y & =0 \\ y(3y-1) & =0 \\ y & =0,\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the corresponding points are $(0,0)$ and $(0,\frac{1}{3}).$"} {:db/id 17592186375335 :question/id #uuid "703e7046-bcfc-54c8-9bb1-c367d4d9ddb7" :question/math-academy-id "q-72427"} {:db/id :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4xy & =-5{x}^{2}+1 \\ {y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2})j \\  & =2(y-2x)\,i-(10x-4y)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ (2(y-2x)\,i-(10x-4y)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2(y-2x) & =0 \\ y & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=2x$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4xy+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ (2x)^{2}-4x(2x)+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ 4{x}^{2}-8{x}^{2}+5{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=1$, we get $y=2$ and the corresponding point is $(1,2).$

- If $x=-1$, we get $y=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,-2).$"} {:db/id 17592186447371 :question/id #uuid "2ac861e6-ea7e-53f0-b9c2-bba93cd70561" :question/math-academy-id "q-130227"} {:db/id :topic/math-academy-id 1940} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125292 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125733 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the equation of the **tangent line** to the ellipse 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac{y^2}{4} =1
$$

 at the point $P(3,1).$

To solve this problem, we could find the slope of the line using techniques from single-variable calculus. However, we can also solve the problem by computing the gradient of a two-variable function.

Let's start by defining 

$$
f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac {y^2}{4}.
$$

Then, the given ellipse is the level curve  $f(x,y)=1.$

Now, we know that $\nabla \! f(3,1)$ is a vector that's normal to the level curve $f(x,y)= 1$ at $P(3,1).$ So, it's also normal to the tangent line to our ellipse at $P.$

![](images/3d/3dc75e8fd4083af1bf90f46b2e875d5d552bffdc5c1cfaeabebef70f79f00828.png)

Suppose that $(x,y)$ is any point on that tangent line. Then $\mathbf v=\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle$ is a vector that's parallel to the tangent line. So $\mathbf v$ must be also orthogonal to $\nabla f(3,1),$ and since the dot product of two orthogonal vectors is zero, we have that

$$
\nabla f(3,1)\,\cdot \,\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle = 0.
$$

Now, computing $\nabla\! f$ and evaluating it at the point $P(3,1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{x}{6},\frac{y}{2}⟩ \\ ∇\,f(3,1) & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the equation of our tangent, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(3,1)\cdot ⟨x-3,y-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y-1⟩ & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}(x-3)+\frac{1}{2}(y-1) & =0 \\ (x-3)+(y-1) & =0 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7a9dede8-0672-56eb-9084-cf581e3fb05f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2496 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7cc9655e-83bb-5f85-8c20-add1d27fb5e0" :step/math-academy-id 11184 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125464}} {:db/id 17592186125293 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124454 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124258 :question/id #uuid "a01560be-9023-593a-87d3-7412f3b208a3" :question/math-academy-id "e-3362"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5ae7e9c8-60e9-5f5e-afbf-1de6bb01bf07" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050027}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124979} {:db/id 17592186125075} {:db/id 17592186265823} {:db/id 17592186265826} {:db/id 17592186339099} {:db/id 17592186388076} {:db/id 17592186393208} {:db/id 17592186447370} {:db/id 17592186447373} {:db/id 17592186459277}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Tangent Line to a Level Curve"} :step/id #uuid "204027bd-d606-5131-82eb-717c2823cc14" :step/math-academy-id 11185 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125294}} {:db/id 17592186125294 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125734 :tutorial/content "Given a level curve $f(x,y) = f(x_0,y_0),$ a **tangent vector** is

$$
\mathbf t(x_0,y_0) = f_y(x_0,y_0) \ \mathbf i - f_x(x_0,y_0) \ \mathbf j.
$$

 

To understand why the above vector is tangent to the level curve, first recall that the gradient vector $\nabla f(x_0,y_0)$ is normal to the level curve. Now, by computing the dot product, we see that the vector $\mathbf t$ is orthogonal to the gradient vector $\nabla\! f{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f\cdot t & =({f}_{x}\text{ }i+{f}_{y}\text{ }j)\cdot ({f}_{y}\text{ }i-{f}_{x}j) \\  & ={f}_{x}{f}_{y}-{f}_{y}{f}_{x} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $\mathbf t$ is tangent to the level curve." :tutorial/id #uuid "6ef07808-783a-543e-9217-5d3d0a9ae13a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2497 :tutorial/title "The Tangent Vector to a Plane $$
f(x,y)= f(x_0,y_0)
$$

$$
\nabla\! f (x_0,y_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0,y-y_0\rangle  = 0.
$$

$$
f_x(x_0,y_0)(x-x_0) + f_y(x_0,y_0)(y-y_0)   = 0.

:topic/math-academy-id 3708} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186180479 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180713 :tutorial/content "The line integral with respect to $x$ of the function $f(x,y)$ along the path $C$ can be calculated using the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t,
$$

where $\mathbf r (t)$ for $a\leq t\leq b$ is a parametrization of $C.$ 

Now, if we set $f(x,y) = 1,$ then by the change of variables formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}_{2}-{x}_{1},\end{aligned}
$$

where $x_1$ and $x_2$ are the $x$-coordinates at the initial and terminal points of $C,$ respectively. To summarize,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d x = x_2 - x_1.
$$

Let's use this result to calculate $\displaystyle\int_C\,\textrm d x,$ where $C$ is the path along the quarter-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O$ in the first quadrant, traversed in the clockwise direction, as shown below:

![](images/01/01b5f21b2c778f62f7dd884065ee4ce17dd01bd021063fc7c788f09a89feea86.png)

The initial point is $(0,2)$ and the terminal point is $(2,0).$ So, we have $x_1 = 0, x_2 = 2,$ and therefore,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d x = 2-0 = 2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c57d3ca1-3c93-5d88-8e4f-5bee849ea14e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5814 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e23b5a77-ead0-581f-bcc1-2f32ba803361" :step/math-academy-id 17592186180483 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180714 :tutorial/content "In addition, we note the following regarding line integrals with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

- If $C = C_1\cup C_2$ is a piecewise-smooth curve, then

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = \int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x +  \int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x.
$$

- When $C$ is a *closed* curve, we sometimes use the following notation:

$$
\oint_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x
$$

 
If the curve is traversed once, the initial and terminal points are the same, so $x_1 = x_2.$ Therefore, for line integrals of unity with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\oint_C \,\textrm d x = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7c1ae4ef-4256-598c-b44d-3421c8c4ebe1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5817 :tutorial/title "Some Remarks"} :step/id #uuid "b7182be2-ddc6-5d8c-9367-0bf313338059" :step/math-academy-id 35673 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180480}} {:db/id 17592186180484 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180715 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we showed that

$$
\int_{C}\,\textrm d x = 2,
$$

where $C$ is the path along the quarter-circle shown below.

![](images/01/01b5f21b2c778f62f7dd884065ee4ce17dd01bd021063fc7c788f09a89feea86.png)

If we reverse the orientation of the curve, we get the following path:

![](images/46/469675e85a6ca1d23de6da985d36e8e86c859ceff38ea6849984ea3c2cd34abe.png)

The initial and terminal points have swapped, and so we now have $x_1 = 2$ and $x_2 = 0.$ Applying our formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-C}\,\text{d}x & ={x}_{2}-{x}_{1} \\  & =0-2 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

This example illustrates an important property of line integrals with respect to $x,$ described in full as follows:

*Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth path in the $xy$-plane, and let $-C$ be the curve consisting of the same points as $C$ but with the opposite orientation. Then,*

$$
\displaystyle\int_{-C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = -\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x.
$$

*Similarly, *

$$
\displaystyle\int_{-C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d y = -\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d y.
$$

In other words, line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y$ are *dependent on orientation*. This is quite different from the case for line integrals with respect to arc length, which are independent of orientation." :tutorial/id #uuid "6fb52502-a498-5599-851c-64cf19d11bf3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5818 :tutorial/title "Further Properties of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y"} :step/id #uuid "fb92124a-a40c-5b95-8acb-21f039c39f10" :step/math-academy-id 35674 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180482}} {:db/id 17592186180485 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180716 :tutorial/content "Similar to line integrals of unity with respect to $x,$ the line integral of unity with respect to $y$ along a path $C$ is equal to the net change in $y$ between the terminal and initial points:

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d y = y_2 - y_1,
$$

where $y_2$ is the $y$-coordinate of the terminal point, and $y_1$ is the $y$-coordinate of the initial point. 

Also, if $C$ is a closed, positively oriented curve traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, then

$$
\oint_C \,\textrm d y = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "16485104-9964-58c8-8611-2769190cbf9c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5819 :tutorial/title "Line Integrals of Unity With Respect to Y"} :step/id #uuid "e5542a0f-35f9-5d2c-a937-679f3e3b6ef6" :step/math-academy-id 35675 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180481}} {:db/id 17592186180486 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180717 :tutorial/content "![](images/c2/c2ab6be66d91822186ee94c846f8cd1a247da776b89d7d9220b836193b9b04d3.png)

Consider the path $C$ above. Earlier, we showed that

$$
\int_{C}\,\textrm d x = 2,
$$

We note the following:

- In the context of our usual interpretation of line integrals with respect to $x,$ this result represents the total area accumulated when the function $z=1$ is projected onto the plane $y=0$ as $C$ is traversed from the initial point $(0,2)$ to the terminal point $(2,0).$ 

![](images/29/297e4e302b0cec7f4448ec7e8b36ab6c1f84d79d5f71aad1c6887d86d54dc328.png)

From the diagram, we see that this projection generates a rectangle of length $x_2 - x_1 = 2$ and height $z=1.$ Since the integral of unity with respect to $x$ along $C$ is equal to the area of this rectangle, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}x & =1\cdot ({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}) \\  & ={x}_{2}-{x}_{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Furthermore, this result is *positive* because the rectangle is traced out in the direction of *increasing* $x.$

- If we reverse the direction of the curve then we get a *negative* result. This is because the rectangle is traced out in the direction of *decreasing* $x,$ as shown below.

![](images/17/179713734445f85818ef4e46cfa5948115cea936538acd3095cbfa706d381972.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "1ba2d901-3b8c-5ce9-a7bd-ace7643f3277" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5820 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind Some of the Results"} :step/id #uuid "a896d261-9315-51e1-80bb-4191a37e68b3" :step/math-academy-id 35676}] :activity/title "Properties of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179861} {:db/id 17592186180479 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180713 :tutorial/content "The line integral with respect to $x$ of the function $f(x,y)$ along the path $C$ can be calculated using the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t,
$$

where $\mathbf r (t)$ for $a\leq t\leq b$ is a parametrization of $C.$ 

Now, if we set $f(x,y) = 1,$ then by the change of variables formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}_{2}-{x}_{1},\end{aligned}
$$

where $x_1$ and $x_2$ are the $x$-coordinates at the initial and terminal points of $C,$ respectively. To summarize,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d x = x_2 - x_1.
$$

Let's use this result to calculate $\displaystyle\int_C\,\textrm d x,$ where $C$ is the path along the quarter-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O$ in the first quadrant, traversed in the clockwise direction, as shown below:

![](images/01/01b5f21b2c778f62f7dd884065ee4ce17dd01bd021063fc7c788f09a89feea86.png)

The initial point is $(0,2)$ and the terminal point is $(2,0).$ So, we have $x_1 = 0, x_2 = 2,$ and therefore,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d x = 2-0 = 2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c57d3ca1-3c93-5d88-8e4f-5bee849ea14e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5814 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e23b5a77-ead0-581f-bcc1-2f32ba803361" :step/math-academy-id 35641 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180483}} {:db/id 17592186180713 :tutorial/content "The line integral with respect to $x$ of the function $f(x,y)$ along the path $C$ can be calculated using the formula

${\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y$ given that $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}$ be a piecewise smooth path in the $xy$-plane, and let $-C$ be the curve consisting of the same points as $C$ but with the opposite orientation. 

For line integrals with respect to $y,$ we have the following properties:

- ${\int }_{-C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y=-{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y$

- ${\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{-{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =-3+5 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "057ed5af-875f-53e1-addf-521f93615e7d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186426493}} {:db/id 17592186426491 :step/content {:db/id 17592186259672 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "55c54a1b-25be-5636-b467-f5ac1a9b52a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186257520} {:answer/id #uuid "90ca79dc-a39f-5a16-a0bb-06f5058a2325" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186258059} {:answer/id #uuid "90fced00-d179-5243-b71b-5f2af240f1e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5+5\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186258062} {:answer/id #uuid "f4d9b801-9124-53be-9f21-3845b38cdb84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186258919} {:answer/id #uuid "f8d92c55-a2da-5101-b6a0-b111b36b6752" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186258966}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186258919} :answer-field/id #uuid "4daa3094-63d7-51fd-af1c-c3ff26a2ec4f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186259167}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6bbf9141-617f-5455-b7c6-ab9b0397e741" :question/math-academy-id "q-124336" :question/problem "![](images/cb/cbef822c90e494cbe75e4a0b4ef93b058fccdd0111ec997f13930b1dba44406d.png)

$$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}],\,v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $v$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** $v$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$
- **II.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$
- **III.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{2}$ of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{1}\ne 0.$ Recall that an *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

With this in mind, let's examine our statements.

First, we compute $A-2I:$

$$
A-2I=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- Next, we find the image of $v$ under the action of $A-2I:$

$$
(A-2I)v=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\ne 0
$$

- Since we got a nonzero vector in the last step, we now compute the image of $w$ under the action of $A-2I:$

$$
(A-2I)w=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 5\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=0
$$

So, we obtain the following chain of maps:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{v}\overset{\,A-2I\,\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\overset{\,A-2I\,\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{0}
$$

Here, we see that $A-2I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $2$ steps.

Therefore:

$\,$ *$v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A.$*

So, the correct answer is "III only.""} {:db/id 17592186433716 :question/id #uuid "93f4dbff-c62f-571f-9c49-e5503854925a" :question/math-academy-id "q-109518"} {:db/id 17592186433717 :question/id #uuid 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
\begin{aligned}u\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }v\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }w\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 \\ x\overset{\,\,\,A\,\,\,\,}{\to }y\overset{\,\,\,A\,\,\,\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Given the action of the matrices $A-5I$ and $A$ on the nonzero vectors $u,v,w,x$ and $y$ as depicted above, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $v$ is a generalized  eigenvector of rank $2$  corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5$ of $A$

- **II.** $y$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ of $A$

- **III.** $u$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5$ of $A$" :question/worked-solution "A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{n}$ of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{n}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{n-1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }…\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since 

$$
v\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }w\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A-5I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $2$ steps, 
the vector $v$ is an generalized eigenvector of rank $2$  corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5$ of $A.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since

$$
y\overset{\,\,\,A\,\,\,\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A=A-0I$ maps $y$ to $0$ in $1$ step, 
the vector $y$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ (a.k.a. an eigenvector) corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ of $A.$

- Statement III is false. Since

$$
u\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }v\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }w\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A-5I$ maps $u$ to $0$ in $3$ steps, 
the vector $u$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3,$ not $4.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} {:db/id 17592186244251 :question/id #uuid "2cf2c42d-88e3-50f2-bb3a-16ab087d4389" :question/math-academy-id "q-109236"} {:db/id 17592186244253 :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
\begin{aligned}v\overset{A+20I\,}{\to }w\overset{A+20I\,}{\to }0 \\ x\overset{A-15I\,}{\to }y\overset{A-15I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Given the action of the matrices $A+20I$ and $A-15I$ on the nonzero vectors $v,w,x$ and $y$ as depicted above, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $v$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-20$ of $A$
- **II.** $x$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =15$ of $A$
- **III.** $w$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-20$ of $A$" :question/worked-solution "A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{n}$ of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{n}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{n-1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }…\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Since 

$$
v\overset{A+20I\,}{\to }w,
$$

and $w\ne 0,$  the vector $v$ is  **not** a eigenvector corresponding  to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-20$  of $A.$

- Statement II is false. Since

$$
x\overset{A-15I\,}{\to }y\overset{A-15I\,}{\to }0,
$$

 
i.e. $A-15I$ maps $x$ to $0$ in $2$ steps, 
the vector $x$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2,$ not $3.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since

$$
w\overset{A+20I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A+20I$ maps $w$ to $0$ in $1$ step, 
the vector $w$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ (a.k.a. an eigenvector) corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-20$ of $A.$

Given the action of the matrices $A+3I$ and $A-3I$ on the nonzero vectors $u,v,w,x$ and $y$ as depicted above, which of the following statements are true?

- **I.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ of $A$

- **III.** $y$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A$" :question/worked-solution "A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{n}$ of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since 

$$
v\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }w\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A+3I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $2$ steps, 
the vector $v$ is a generalized  eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ of $A.$

$$
u\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }v\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }w\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A+3I$ maps $u$ to $0$ in $3$ steps, 
the vector $u$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3,$ not $2.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since

$$
y\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A-3I$ maps $y$ to $0$ in $1$ step, 
the vector $y$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A.$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 & 2 \\ 4 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $v$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** $v$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$
- **II.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$
- **III.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{n}$ of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{n}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{n-1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }…\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

First, we compute $A-2I:$

$$
A-2I=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 & 2 \\ 4 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

- Next, we find the image of $v$ under the action of $A-2I:$

$$
(A-2I)v=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\ne 0
$$

- Since we got a nonzero vector in the last step, we now compute the image of $w$ under the action of $A-2I:$

$$
(A-2I)w=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=0
$$

So, we obtain the following chain of maps:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{v}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{0}
$$

Here, we see that $A-2I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $2$ steps.

Therefore:

$\,$ *$v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A.$*

So, the correct answer is "II only.""} {:db/id 17592186247002 :question/id #uuid "1069f3ce-ee29-5917-b7ea-2041ea76b45b" :question/math-academy-id "q-109525" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b486bce2-fa4e-513e-b610-7ee71b9233d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186461581} {:answer/id #uuid "c967c74a-a0ee-5cb2-add3-5fb704306c38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186461582}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186461581} :answer-field/id #uuid "2da9584a-9261-5bdd-a02e-94d0f8f396e9" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186462544} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "97da4738-01b7-5e07-a794-eb18f27e9287" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186461583} {:answer/id #uuid "89d9db19-d46a-585f-b48b-56f4ec6588cf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186461584}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186461583} :answer-field/id #uuid "34cf3572-0f16-58e0-891b-e7abf95b07a2" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186462545} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "378a528d-b550-5f7a-974c-a7e21760d896" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186461585} {:answer/id #uuid "0b31d8dd-5d0d-5f38-aee8-7880656f4805" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186461586}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186461586} :answer-field/id #uuid "5bcc4b93-4a4f-5d15-a1a8-5b17a48be491" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186462546}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{n}$ of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{n}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{n-1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }…\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

First, we compute $A-I:$

$$
A-I=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- Next, we find the image of $v$ under the action of $A-I:$

$$
(A-I)v=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\ne 0
$$

- Since we got a nonzero vector in the last step, we now compute the image of $w$ under the action of $A-I:$

$$
(A-I)w=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=0
$$

So, we obtain the following chain of maps:

$$

- **I.** $v$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =8$ of $A$
- **II.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =8$ of $A$
- **III.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =8$ of $A$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{n}$ of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{n}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{n-1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }…\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

First, we compute $A-8I:$

$$
A-8I=[\begin{aligned}9 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 9 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

- Next, we find the image of $v$ under the action of $A-8I:$

$$
(A-8I)v=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4 \\ 8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\ne 0
$$

- Since we got a nonzero vector in the last step, we now compute the image of $w$ under the action of $A-8I:$

$$
(A-8I)w=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4 \\ 8\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=0
$$

So, we obtain the following chain of maps:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{v}\overset{A-8I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4 \\ 8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\overset{A-8I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{0}
$$

Here, we see that $A-8I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $2$ steps.

Therefore:

$\,$ *$v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =8$ of $A.$*

Recall that a nonzero vector $\mathbf{v}_1$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda$ if

$$
A\mathbf{v}_1 = \lambda \mathbf{v}_1.
$$

We can write this equation as 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{0}.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A-\lambda I$ maps the vector $\mathbf{v}_1$ to the zero vector $\mathbf{0}{:}$

$$
\mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \mathbf{0}
$$

Now suppose that there exists a nonzero vector $\mathbf v_2$ that is mapped to the zero vector in *two* steps by the matrix $A-\lambda I.$ That is,

$$
(A-\lambda I)\mathbf v_2 = \mathbf v_1 \qquad \textrm{and}\qquad (A-\lambda I)\mathbf v_1 = \mathbf 0,
$$

where $\mathbf v_1$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda.$

We can represent this schematically as a chain of mappings, as follows:

$$
\mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \mathbf{v}_{1} \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I}  \mathbf{0}
$$

We call $\mathbf v_2$ a **generalized eigenvector of rank** $2$ because it is mapped to the zero vector in two steps. 

By the same idea, an eigenvector of $A$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ because it is mapped to the zero vector in one step." :tutorial/id #uuid "88994c46-d16a-531c-895a-e2c3fdddfc1f" "q-109434" :question/problem "$$
\begin{aligned}s\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }u\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }v\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }w\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 \\ x\overset{\,\,\,A\,\,\,\,}{\to }y\overset{\,\,\,A\,\,\,\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Given the action of the matrices $A-4I$ and $A$ on the nonzero vectors $s,u,v,w,x$ and $y$ as depicted above, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $s$ is a generalized  eigenvector of rank $4$  corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ of $A$
- **II.** $x$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ of $A$
- **III.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ of $A$" :question/worked-solution "A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{n}$ of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{n}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{n-1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }…\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since 

$$
s\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }u\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }v\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }w\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A-4I$ maps $s$ to $0$ in $4$ steps, 
the vector $s$ is an generalized eigenvector of rank $4$  corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ of $A.$

- Statement II is false. Since

$$
x\overset{\,\,\,A\,\,\,\,}{\to }y\overset{\,\,\,A\,\,\,\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A=A-0I$ maps $x$ to $0$ in $2$ steps, 
the vector $x$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2,$ not $1.$

- Statement III is false. Since

$$
v\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }w\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A-4I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $2$ steps, 
the vector $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2,$ not $3.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} :step/id #uuid "2bc8515b-cb7e-52c2-b2ca-3e1502bf57b3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186413003}} {:db/id 17592186413002 :step/content {:db/id 17592186412998 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8610a0d2-fdc1-5ffb-bb7d-fa4d5ec60050" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453246} {:answer/id #uuid "1106162e-004a-5376-84ea-4d09f59735a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453247}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453247} :answer-field/id #uuid "16308504-1737-59ec-85f8-6aae9a6e62ca" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454373} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "654b12c7-247f-59a8-b59b-c9aa7e6df741" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453248} {:answer/id #uuid "d1caa7bb-f241-5fda-a091-982727ce423c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453249}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453248} :answer-field/id #uuid "dec4b167-b790-52bb-b09f-3c495acb1957" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454374} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7fb38f24-ce58-5679-8e4c-5ab1475e60b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453250} {:answer/id #uuid "c9beb16d-fb59-5d8a-9e62-f88859d6a643" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453251}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453251} :answer-field/id #uuid "291c74d0-3740-5390-9af2-8599a8ba49e9" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454375}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "28941d92-3462-55d4-9376-780e240021c7" :question/math-academy-id "q-109277" :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $v$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** $v$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$
- **II.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$
- **III.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{2}$ of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{1}\ne 0.$ Recall that an *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

With this in mind, let's examine our statements.

First, we compute $A-2I:$

$$
A-2I=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- Next, we find the image of $v$ under the action of $A-2I:$

$$
(A-2I)v=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\ne 0
$$

- Since we got a nonzero vector in the last step, we now compute the image of $w$ under the action of $A-2I:$

$$
(A-2I)w=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 5\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=0
$$

So, we obtain the following chain of maps:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{v}\overset{\,A-2I\,\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\overset{\,A-2I\,\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{0}
$$

Here, we see that $A-2I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $2$ steps.

Therefore:

$\,$ *$v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of $A.$*

So, the correct answer is "III only.""} :step/id #uuid "ea9a4e19-af76-5650-86a8-7d1214ec77ba"}] :activity/title "Generalized Eigenvectors" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident $$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

First, we compute $A+2I:$

$$
A+2I=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -5 & 1 \\ 4 & -9 & 1\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -9 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

- Next, we find the image of $v$ under the action of $A+2I:$

$$
(A+2I)v=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -9 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\ne 0
$$

- Since we got a nonzero vector, we now compute the image of $w$ under the action of $A+2I:$

$$
(A+2I)w=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -9 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}\ne 0
$$

- Again, since we got a nonzero vector in the last step, we now compute the image of $x$ under the action of $A+2I:$

$$
(A+2I)x=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -9 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=0
$$

So, we obtain the following chain of maps:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{v}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{0}
$$

Here, we see that $A+2I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $3$ steps.

17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "28941d92-3462-55d4-9376-780e240021c7" :question/math-academy-id "q-109277" :question/problem "$$
\begin{aligned}u\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }v\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }w\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }0 \\ x\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }y\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Given the action of the matrices $A+3I$ and $A-3I$ on the nonzero vectors $u,v,w,x$ and $y$ as depicted above, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ of $A$

- **II.** $u$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ of $A$

- **III.** $y$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A$" :question/worked-solution "A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{n}$ of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{n}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{n-1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }…\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since 

$$
v\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }w\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A+3I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $2$ steps, 
the vector $v$ is a generalized  eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3$ of $A.$

- Statement II is false. Since

$$
u\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }v\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }w\overset{A+3I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A+3I$ maps $u$ to $0$ in $3$ steps, 
the vector $u$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3,$ not $2.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since

$$
y\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0,
$$

i.e. $A-3I$ maps $y$ to $0$ in $1$ step, 
the vector $y$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "af00e671-378f-5ae3-95bf-22f18e729b56" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436619}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials can be used for solving homogeneous systems of the form

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix.

For example, consider the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](images/f9/f94140f8c9fe736ca7c574547658856e85d938eb08064046716be8eb1a2748de.svg)
where ![](images/26/26dcf2c367c915460d09f4f38b40e4f792a06b6ab44291b4739a6935529daf89.svg) So, the matrix of the system is ![](images/90/9000e03ddf617a1e3c4e0eed5da2b846d62e3d68588b601d90643783960d17df.svg)

Recall that given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is some constant vector.

Since we have already seen how to compute the standard fundamental matrix, we will not repeat the calculation here. So, computing the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system, we get
![](images/11/11e0da79656b7f8e2c84c6c54e6dd6b54cf53cbb8e746d44dfb13329c3d2ed8f.svg)

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$

**Note:** Recall that for the general solution of the ordinary differential equation $x'(t)=ax(t),$ we have 

$$
x'(t)=ax(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
x(t) = c \, e^{at}, 
\quad
c \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Now, for the general solution of the matrix differential equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ we obtain 

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \, \mathbf{c},
\quad
\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^n.
$$

Let's see more examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "978fc2f4-910c-5bef-9ae3-3da9377642ce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14515 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c774d65b-c500-58e4-aa9a-e222d3d136ae" :step/math-academy-id 592270 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230003}} {:db/id 17592186230003 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229142 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228910 :question/id #uuid "26df399d-cd87-5b5d-9f3f-7ced4ca5fd06" :question/math-academy-id "e-21707"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e5bc609b-dc5b-52e9-9f0e-206f32bb829b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050125} {:db/id 17592186050228}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186229669} {:db/id 17592186229677} {:db/id 17592186308684} {:db/id 17592186308685} {:db/id 17592186402113} {:db/id 17592186445608} {:db/id 17592186445610} {:db/id 17592186445613}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the General Solution of a Homogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential"} :step/id #uuid "d3b52974-38d7-50fa-b648-b51510a9a617" :step/math-academy-id 592271 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230004}} {:db/id 17592186230004 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230193 :tutorial/content "Now, let's find the solution to the initial value problem below

1\. *Law of Exponents:* If $A$ is a constant square matrix, then

  $$
  e^{A(t+s)} = e^{At}\,e^{As}.
  $$

2\. *Inverse:* For any $t,$ the matrix $e^{At}$ is invertible and 

  $$
  (e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}.
  $$

3\. *Identity:* For any square matrix $A,$

  $$
  e^{A\cdot 0} = I.
  $$

4\. *Product of exponentials:* If $A$ and $B$ commute (i.e., $AB = BA$), then

  $$
  e^{A}e^{B} = e^{A+B}.
  $$

  **Watch out!** In general, this identity is *not true* unless $A$ and $B$ commute.

Let's see how these properties can be used in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "5ae3cfa7-a5a5-5a50-aefa-8b8dec561567" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14528 :tutorial/title "Reminder: Properties of Matrix Exponentials"} :step/id #uuid "eb56047e-3845-5f8e-9282-d41f308270e3" :step/math-academy-id 592282 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230009}} {:db/id 17592186230009 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229145 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228911 :question/id #uuid "ace067cd-e1d0-5b3e-bae2-bf58dcac3585" :question/math-academy-id "e-21711"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1ff837c0-0ebb-5a9e-acb4-894261e0318c" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186229658} {:db/id 17592186229697} {:db/id 17592186311712} {:db/id 17592186311794} {:db/id 17592186311799} {:db/id 17592186372710} {:db/id 17592186396936} {:db/id 17592186396993} {:db/id 17592186445612} {:db/id 17592186445614}] :knowledge-point/title "Proving the Matrix Exponential Formula for IVP Solution: Homogeneous Systems"} :step/id #uuid "6a90e198-ec80-5daf-8cb9-69841a16a32d" :step/math-academy-id 592283}] :activity/title "Solving Homogeneous Systems of ODEs Using Matrix Methods" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186229256} {:db/id 17592186230002 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230188 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials can be used for solving homogeneous systems of the form

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix.

For example, consider the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](images/f9/f94140f8c9fe736ca7c574547658856e85d938eb08064046716be8eb1a2748de.svg)
where ![](images/26/26dcf2c367c915460d09f4f38b40e4f792a06b6ab44291b4739a6935529daf89.svg) So, the matrix of the system is ![](images/90/9000e03ddf617a1e3c4e0eed5da2b846d62e3d68588b601d90643783960d17df.svg)

Recall that given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is some constant vector.

Since we have already seen how to compute the standard fundamental matrix, we will not repeat the calculation here. So, computing the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system, we get
![](images/11/11e0da79656b7f8e2c84c6c54e6dd6b54cf53cbb8e746d44dfb13329c3d2ed8f.svg)

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$

**Note:** Recall that for the general solution of the ordinary differential equation $x'(t)=ax(t),$ we have 

$$
x'(t)=ax(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
x(t) = c \, e^{at}, 
\quad
c \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Now, for the general solution of the matrix differential equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ we obtain 

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \, \mathbf{c},
\quad
\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^n.
$$

given that ![](images/ee/ee25228bf71d1b7d9d0688af06a7f1335c252310127b403ed0ed37f7fe277c07.svg) where ![](images/3a/3a3ac9326741c0e2390a8e2f079808f0b432b740149ef4b034ffa7568dc33848.svg)

Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](images/2b/2b81cf358ffb3df49f327b63138640ac452a249f989353b521be34d531aeffd9.svg)
where ![](images/11/1110f0bdbe784b21683bfb9610ca9c04e5a45755954d49a15124e530feef2002.svg) So, the matrix of the system is ![](images/47/47d8a0214e5ccdf6625a330d23003dec11cbc3a4f35cb2992df29a688963e4b2.svg)

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution is $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \, \mathbf{c}.$ We can determine the constant vector $\mathbf{c}$ using the initial condition at time $t=t_0{:}$

$$
\mathbf{x}(t_0) = e^{At_0} \, \mathbf{c} \implies \mathbf{c} = e^{-At_0} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0),
$$

since the inverse of $e^{At_0}$ is $e^{-At_0}.$ Plugging this back into our general solution gives the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our specific problem (with $t_0=1$) is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-1)) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-1)) \\ -4\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0fe9a975-9d92-5f79-8a67-34af55196fb3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14530 :tutorial/title "Solving Initial Value Problems With Shifted Conditions"} {:db/id 17592186230007 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229144 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228917 :question/id #uuid "b061f2b1-b015-582f-921f-9b444db631ee" :question/math-academy-id "e-21723"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "37e58bb6-6d90-5171-bba2-6ffa5a0c91d9" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186229664} {:db/id 17592186229684} {:db/id 17592186311564} {:db/id 17592186311590} {:db/id 17592186311591} {:db/id 17592186311592} {:db/id 17592186311593} {:db/id 17592186311594} {:db/id 17592186391579} {:db/id 17592186391586} {:db/id 17592186445615}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential: Shifted Initial Conditions"} :step/id #uuid "633a401e-5116-5c9e-a0b4-8848cf596d7b" :step/math-academy-id 592279 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230008}} {:db/id 17592186230008 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230192 :tutorial/content "Before proceeding with the next example, let's recall some important properties of matrix exponentials:

1\. *Law of Exponents:* If $A$ is a constant square matrix, then

  $$
  e^{A(t+s)} = e^{At}\,e^{As}.
  $$

2\. *Inverse:* For any $t,$ the matrix $e^{At}$ is invertible and 

  $$
  (e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}.
  $$

3\. *Identity:* For any square matrix $A,$

  $$
  e^{A\cdot 0} = I.
  $$

4\. *Product of exponentials:* If $A$ and $B$ commute (i.e., $AB = BA$), then

  $$
  e^{A}e^{B} = e^{A+B}.
  $$

  **Watch out!** In general, this identity is *not true* unless $A$ and $B$ commute.

Let's see how these properties can be used in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "5ae3cfa7-a5a5-5a50-aefa-8b8dec561567" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14528 :tutorial/title "Reminder: Properties of Matrix Exponentials"} :step/id #uuid "eb56047e-3845-5f8e-9282-d41f308270e3" :step/math-academy-id 592282 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230009}} {:db/id 17592186230192 :tutorial/content "Before proceeding with the next example, let's recall some important properties of matrix exponentials:

:question/problem "If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the curves $y=3-{x}^{2}$ and $y=x+1,$ then ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA=$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](images/73/7316d667d7308ac5ec0f5348055d3d0e7eb90b97abaa74f5693c3151dc3b8bb1.png)

Now, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. 

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3-{x}^{2} & =x+1 \\ {x}^{2}+x-2 & =0 \\ (x-1)(x+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x$-limits are 
$-2\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/aa/aab6fb99694b518bfa9d200a75876c9e888ba1ab7d699464bc9caca360be775a.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 1,\,x+1\le y\le 3-{x}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}{\int }_{x+1}^{3-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}[{\int }_{x+1}^{3-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186380943 :question/id #uuid "c17aef4e-54b4-5fd5-b0e4-5e8c5c062f24" :question/math-academy-id "q-132240"} {:db/id 17592186380950 :question/id #uuid "bf1ebc54-3588-5672-a9a8-34aff8268c29" :question/math-academy-id "q-132249"} {:db/id 17592186382476 :question/id #uuid "043f5e2c-ec1d-5bfd-95f4-c3f133eb89cc" :question/math-academy-id "q-81342"} {:db/id 17592186394154 :question/id #uuid "e08c75d3-95c8-54b4-9cdf-5e4550896e07" :question/math-academy-id "q-81336"} {:db/id 17592186408131 :question/id #uuid "3676ec52-02c6-5b83-a547-e552c5ceb042" :question/math-academy-id "q-81338" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "58f2f8c3-eca9-558a-ae7f-9a78208457ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{-{x}^{2}}{\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{2}y-3x)\,dy\,dx" :db/id 17592186408123} {:answer/id #uuid "647e13d7-fe24-5171-9f25-59459873bf42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-{x}^{2}}^{-1}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}y-3x)\,dy\,dx" :db/id 17592186408124} {:answer/id #uuid "93175eb3-2514-5cc0-a423-e088c96ac28d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{-{x}^{2}}({x}^{2}y-3x)\,dy\,dx" :db/id 17592186408125} {:answer/id #uuid "93b1f2e7-cf7b-5b8a-b5bb-c62e89e19fa2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{-{x}^{2}}({x}^{2}y-3x)\,dy\,dx" :db/id 17592186408126} {:answer/id #uuid "ef3be0a4-83b9-54e6-81b8-88c21e425fc7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-{x}^{2}}^{-1}({x}^{2}y-3x)\,dy\,dx" :db/id 17592186408128}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186408126} :answer-field/id #uuid "3df51106-2408-5663-8451-c957471724da" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186408129}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/41/4121d975786de30f34e493e7ac49e5cdc8e66621e800321008ba4ba501fb818f.png)

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dy\,dx=$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x[\,y\,]_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,dx & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-2) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186268854 :question/id #uuid "6f85a13d-0fd8-5d09-bfdb-9a5dcca1ba52" :question/math-academy-id "q-132277"} {:db/id 17592186268855 :question/id #uuid "63aade32-c436-5c43-9ff2-73d45e2de0f9" :question/math-academy-id "q-132282"} {:db/id 17592186323929 :question/id #uuid "39356ac1-0a31-5e6e-9a6f-6a96bbbbe55c" :question/math-academy-id "q-37683" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "04d2a009-9a40-5d25-99e2-4f97af963231" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{11}{4}" :db/id 17592186321192} {:answer/id #uuid "2c533ee8-f9db-5f4a-a560-8035da471b44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6}{11}" :db/id 17592186321490} {:answer/id #uuid "3a0552d2-cfa6-5c1e-901c-be3cad62fa64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{11}" :db/id 17592186321590} {:answer/id #uuid "70ec84ef-6655-53bf-9eb0-7897a3753db2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{6}" :db/id 17592186322030} {:answer/id #uuid "80d50f5a-f000-539b-a1db-5c8a13952505" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{12}" :db/id 17592186322160}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322160} :answer-field/id #uuid "4b2db87a-5385-53da-8e27-89a6fe772ff2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323309}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Calculate ${\int }_{1/2}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1/x}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,dy\,dx.$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type I region.
